headings: Choosing a variety: small plant, small pot, big success
The soil: why dirt from outside fails in a pot

Healthy or struggling? What to look for
What can go wrong (and what it means)
docs.text: # Your First Tomato You can grow a real tomato plant with no yard, no experience, and very little money. One plant, one pot, one sunny spot: a windowsill that gets strong sun, a balcony, a doorstep. This guide walks you through the whole season, from choosing a plant to eating something you grew yourself. One honest thing first: your first plant may struggle or even die. That is normal and not wasted; every gardener killed plants while learning. The plant is the lesson, the tomatoes are the bonus. ## What you need Cheapest options first. Much of this can be free, and none of it needs to be fancy. - A container. A 5-gallon food-grade bucket (restaurants and bakeries often give these away) with holes drilled in the bottom works as well as a bought pot. Otherwise, any pot at least 10 inches across for a cherry tomato; 12 to 14 inches (about 4 to 5 gallons) is easier to keep watered and suits almost any container variety. - A bag of potting mix, enough to fill your container. Sold as "potting mix" or "container mix." Not "garden soil" and not "topsoil." More on why below. - One young tomato plant (called a "transplant" or "start"), a few inches tall, from a garden center, hardware store, or a neighbor. Buying a plant instead of seeds skips the hardest weeks; seeds are cheaper but add weeks of fussy indoor care and an extra way to fail. - A small stake or tomato cage if your variety grows taller than about 2 feet. Many patio types stay short and need nothing. - Vegetable fertilizer, any cheap one. The package shows three numbers (the nutrient mix). Avoid ones where the FIRST number is the biggest; 5-10-10 or anything labeled "for tomatoes" is fine, and an all-equal mix like 10-10-10 also works. ## Choosing a variety: small plant, small pot, big success Tomato varieties range from compact bushes to sprawling vines taller than you are. For a container, you want the compact end: - Cherry tomatoes: small fruit, lots of it, earliest to ripen, and the most forgiving. Container-friendly names include Tumbler, Tumbling Tom, Tiny Tim, and Terenzo. - Patio types: bred specifically for pots. Names like Patio, Patio Choice, and Patio Princess. Some stay only 18 inches tall. - Compact "bush" slicers, like Bush Early Girl, if you want bigger fruit. Skip anything labeled "indeterminate" (a vine that keeps growing all season); it needs a bigger pot and constant tying-up. Labels saying "determinate," "bush," "patio," or "container" are good territory. ## The container: size and drainage Two rules, both absolute: 1. Big enough. At minimum a 2-gallon, 10-inch pot for a cherry type; 4 to 5 gallons is more forgiving for anything. A too-small pot dries out in hours on a hot day. 2. Drainage holes in the bottom. Non-negotiable. Water must be able to run out, or the roots sit in a puddle and rot. If your container has no holes, drill or punch several. Put a saucer or tray under the pot if it lives on a windowsill or balcony you care about. ## The soil: why dirt from outside fails in a pot Use potting mix, not soil dug from the ground. In a pot, garden dirt compacts into a dense brick that drains poorly yet also dries out fast, and it carries weed seeds, insects, and plant diseases. Potting mix is a fluffy blend (usually peat or coir plus perlite, the little white specks) designed to hold moisture and air at the same time. It is the cheapest insurance you can buy for this project. ## Light: the real requirement Tomatoes need direct sun, at least 6 hours a day, and they prefer 8 to 10. This is the requirement people most want to bargain with, and the plant will not bargain; a bright-looking room can offer far less real sun than you think. Before planting, watch your intended spot for a day and honestly count the hours direct sunlight actually lands there. South-facing spots (in the northern hemisphere) are usually best. With less than 6 true hours, a cherry type in your sunniest spot is still worth trying; expect a smaller harvest. ## Planting: the steps Wait until all danger of frost is past and nights are reliably mild. Tomatoes cannot tolerate frost at all, and cold nights below 55 F stall them even without frost. 1. Fill the container with potting mix to a few inches below the rim. 2. Water the mix until water runs out the bottom, then let it drain. 3. Remove the plant from its little pot, loosen the roots gently, and plant it deep, so only the top 2 or 3 sets of leaves stick out above the mix (a set = one leaf-bearing point on the stem; when in doubt, bury about two-thirds of the plant). This feels wrong and is right: tomatoes grow new roots all along a buried stem. Pinch off leaves that would end up underground. 4. Firm the mix around the stem and water again. 5. If using a cage or stake, add it now, not later, so you do not stab established roots. 6. Put the pot in your sunny spot. If your plant came from indoors or a greenhouse, give it a few days of partial sun first so the leaves can toughen up before full sun. Done. ## Watering: the finger test This is the skill that decides how your season goes. Push a finger into the mix down to the second knuckle, about 2 inches. If it feels dry at your fingertip, water slowly until water runs from the drainage holes, then stop. If it feels damp, do nothing and check again tomorrow. That is the whole method. Check daily; in hot summer weather a container tomato can genuinely need water every day, sometimes twice. In cool cloudy weather it may need none for days. The finger decides, not the calendar. The two failure modes are not equal: a wilted, underwatered plant usually recovers within hours of a good drink, but a constantly soggy plant is quietly drowning, because waterlogged roots cannot get air and they rot. Overwatering is the easier mistake, since it comes from caring too much. Consistency also matters as much as amount; wild swings between bone dry and soaked cause the fruit problems below. ## Feeding Potting mix contains little food, so a container tomato must be fed. Two easy approaches, either is fine: - Mix a slow-release fertilizer into the pot at planting, following the package rate, and top up on the package schedule. - Or use a water-soluble fertilizer (dissolved in the watering can) every week or two at the package rate, starting a couple of weeks after planting. More is not better. Too much fertilizer, especially nitrogen-heavy mixes, gives you a huge leafy plant with no tomatoes. Follow the package. When in doubt, feed less. ## Temperature: what the plant can take - Frost kills tomatoes outright. Whenever frost is forecast, or the night will drop near 32 F, bring the pot indoors or cover the plant overnight. This is the container's superpower: unlike a garden, a pot can be picked up and moved. - Fruit set (flowers turning into tomatoes) needs nights above 55 F. Pollination works best between about 70 and 82 F. - In heat waves, fruit set drops off as days climb into the upper 80s and beyond, and ripe red color develops poorly above 90 F. The plant is not dying; it is waiting. In extreme heat you can pick fruit that has started to color and let it finish ripening indoors. ## Healthy or struggling? What to look for A happy plant has deep green leaves, a thick stem, steady new growth at the top, and flowers within a few weeks. Leaves curling a little in midday heat and relaxing by evening is normal. Warning signs: pale or yellowing leaves, a stretched skinny stem leaning toward the light, no new growth for a week, wilting that does not recover overnight, or flowers falling off without fruit. Each appears in the list below. ## What can go wrong (and what it means) - Leggy seedlings (tall, pale, thin, flopping): not enough light. Move the plant to more direct sun and rotate the pot so it stops leaning. When planting a leggy transplant, bury the extra stem deep, as in step 3 above; the flaw becomes roots. - Yellowing lower leaves: a few old bottom leaves yellowing and dropping is normal aging. Many yellow leaves at once usually mean hunger (you skipped feeding) or drowning (soil constantly wet; check your drainage and ease off the watering). - Flowers fall off without fruit (blossom drop): almost always temperature, nights below 55 F or days in the upper 80s and above. You cannot fix the weather; keep the plant watered and fed and it will set fruit when conditions return to normal. - Black leathery sunken patch on the bottom of the fruit (blossom end rot): not a disease, and nothing is eating your plant. The fruit ran short of calcium while forming, which in practice is almost always caused by uneven watering, not bad soil. Remove the affected fruit and water consistently; later fruit will very likely be fine. Sprays are not the fix; steady water is. - Wilting that does not bounce back overnight: check the extremes. If the pot is sitting in a full saucer or the mix is soggy, the roots are drowning; empty the saucer and let the mix dry down. If the mix is bone dry an inch deep, water thoroughly until it drains. Either way, evening recovery within a day or two is the sign you fixed it. - No new growth for a week or more: usually cold nights (growth stalls below the 55 F range) or hunger. If nights are warm and you have not fed the plant in a few weeks, feed it; container mix holds little nutrition on its own. ## Harvest: the payoff A tomato is ready when it reaches full color for its variety (check the label) and feels slightly soft when gently squeezed; ripe fruit twists off the stem easily. Pick cherry types the day they color fully, since they can split if left long, especially after rain. Do not refrigerate a tomato you are about to eat; cold dulls the flavor. ## The honest timeline From planting a purchased transplant to your first ripe fruit is roughly 65 to 90 days for most varieties, with cherry and patio types at the early end. So: plant in late spring, expect your first tomato in mid to late summer. Flowers come first, then green marble-sized fruit, then a long, slightly agonizing wait while they size up and finally color. Nothing is wrong during that wait. The plant then keeps producing until cold weather ends the season. ## What this one plant teaches By the end of one season you will have learned, in your hands and not from a page: how to judge soil moisture, how much sun "full sun" really is, how to read a plant's leaves, and how weather decides what plants do. Those skills transfer to every crop there is. The natural next step is one more container: a second tomato variety to compare, or an easy herb like basil, which loves the same pot, mix, sun, and watering you have already mastered. You are no longer a person who has never grown food. ## Sources University extension services (Iowa State, Clemson, New Hampshire, Maryland, Michigan State, Purdue): - https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/how-to/growing-tomatoes-containers - https://hgic.clemson.edu/tomatoes-in-containers/ - https://extension.unh.edu/blog/2020/01/what-best-way-grow-tomatoes-container - https://extension.umd.edu/resource/growing-tomatoes-home-garden - https://www.canr.msu.edu/resources/blossom_end_rot_tip_sheet - https://www.purdue.edu/hla/sites/yardandgarden/spring-weather-unkind-to-tomatoes/

docs.title: Starting Seeds
headings: What to start indoors, what to sow straight outside
When to start: count backward from your last frost
docs.text: # Starting Seeds If you have grown one plant from a purchased start, the next skill is raising plants from a seed packet yourself. It costs a fraction as much, it opens up hundreds of varieties a store will never stock, and it moves the start of your growing season indoors, onto a windowsill or a shelf, weeks before the weather allows anything outside. One honest thing first: seed starting is the fussiest stage of growing. Seeds fail to sprout, seedlings flop over dead, whole trays go moldy. Every one of those failures has a boring, fixable cause, and all of them are covered below. Losing a tray costs a few cents and two weeks; that is the whole downside. ## Why seeds: the math A packet of seeds typically costs about $1 to $3 and can hold 100 or more seeds. A single young plant (a "transplant" or "start") at a nursery or big-box store runs about $2 to $4, sometimes more. So one packet, even if only half the seeds grow, can produce more plants than most gardens have room for, for less than the price of one bought plant. Prices drift year to year and store to store; the ratio is the point. Leftover seeds keep for later seasons if stored cool and dry. ## What to start indoors, what to sow straight outside Not everything wants an indoor head start. The packet will say which camp a crop is in; here is the pattern: - Start indoors: crops that need a long warm season, longer than most climates provide outdoors. Tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, and onions are the classic list. - Sow direct (straight in the garden): beans, cucumbers, and melons do not transplant well and should go into the ground where they will grow. Carrots and other root crops also go straight in the ground, since the root you eat forms badly if disturbed. Peas are quick and cold-tolerant and are sown outside early. Squash is usually sown direct too, though it can be transplanted young where summers are short. This guide is about the first camp: the indoor start. ## When to start: count backward from your last frost Everything is timed from your area's average last spring frost date. To find yours, search your state extension service's name plus "last frost date," ask your county extension office, or use the National Gardening Association's nationwide zip-code frost date lookup (garden.org/apps/frost-dates). It is an average, not a promise; a late frost can land after it. Then count backward. Weeks of indoor growing before transplant time, by crop: - Lettuce and other leafy greens: 2 to 4 weeks - Cucumber, squash, melon (indoor-start only where summers are too short for direct sowing; disturb the roots as little as possible at transplant): 3 to 5 weeks - Cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower: 4 to 6 weeks - Tomato: 5 to 6 weeks - Pepper, eggplant, onion: 8 to 10 weeks Starting too early is the beginner's classic mistake: you get huge, starved, tangled plants and nowhere to put them. When in doubt, start later. ## What you need Cheapest options first. - Containers, 2 to 3 inches deep. Recycled ones are fine: yogurt cups, cut-down milk jugs, the clear boxes salad greens come in. Two rules: every container must have drainage holes punched in the bottom, and any container that held plants before must be sterilized first (see damping-off below for how). A solid tray underneath, like a baking sheet, catches water and enables bottom watering. - A bag of seed-starting mix. This is not the same as potting mix: it is a finer, lighter, soil-free blend (usually peat and vermiculite) that tiny roots can push through and that starts out free of the organisms that kill seedlings. Buy it new. Never use garden soil or compost for seed starting, and never reuse last year's mix; both carry the damping-off organisms described below. - Seed packets. The packet is your instruction sheet: depth, spacing, days to germinate, and indoor-vs-direct advice are printed on it. - Light. Read the light section below before assuming a window will do. An inexpensive LED or fluorescent shop light on a cheap outlet timer is the reliable answer. - Optional but helpful: a waterproof seedling heat mat (made for damp trays; do not substitute a household heating pad, which is not built to live under wet containers), and labels, because you will not remember which cup is which. ## Sowing: the steps 1. Moisten the mix before filling: dump it in a bucket, add water, and stir until it is damp as a wrung-out sponge, not dripping. 2. Fill the containers, tap them to settle the mix, and set them on the tray. 3. Plant at the right depth. The rule of thumb: a seed goes about twice as deep as it is wide, deep enough that one more seed could sit directly on top of it. Big seeds go a knuckle deep; dust-fine seeds are barely covered or just pressed onto the surface. Too deep is a common cause of nothing coming up. Drop 2 or 3 seeds per container; you will thin to one later. 4. Label each container with the crop and the date. 5. Keep them warm. A potting mix temperature of about 65 to 75 F suits most vegetable seeds; a heat mat holding the mix at 70 to 75 F speeds things up and is itself a damping-off preventer. The top of a refrigerator is the traditional free warm spot. 6. Keep the mix damp, never soggy, and wait. The packet's "days to germinate" number tells you when to expect sprouts and when to start worrying. ## Light: the sunny-window honesty The day sprouts appear, they need strong light, and this is where most first attempts go wrong. A windowsill, even a good south-facing one, usually delivers too few hours of weak, one-sided late-winter light. The result is "leggy" seedlings: tall, pale, thin stems flopping toward the glass. Leggy seedlings are weak seedlings. The fix costs little: a plain LED or fluorescent shop light, hung on adjustable chains or propped so you can raise it. Extension guidance: keep the light close, 2 to 6 inches above the leaf tops, and closer is better (Minnesota Extension advises no more than 4; raise it as the plants grow), and run it 12 to 16 hours a day. An outlet timer makes the hours automatic. Electricity and watering share a shelf here, so name the hazard: keep plugs, timers, and connections up out of any possible drips, water with dry hands, and unplug the light before adjusting its height. If your setup involves rewiring a fixture or an outlet, that is a job for a qualified electrician, not a guess. Seedlings also like it cooler than germinating seeds: roughly 55 to 60 F at night and 65 to 70 F by day grows stockier plants than constant warmth. ## Watering from below Overhead watering flattens seedlings and washes seeds around. Instead, pour water into the solid tray underneath and let the mix drink it up through the drainage holes. When the surface turns dark and damp, pour off whatever still stands in the tray; containers must not sit in a puddle. Water again only when the surface has dried out. Constantly soggy mix is the single biggest invitation to damping-off. ## Thinning: the emotional hurdle You planted 2 or 3 seeds per container, and if you were lucky they all came up. Now cut down all but the strongest one, snipping the extras off at the soil line with scissors. Do not pull them out; pulling tears the roots of the seedling you are keeping. Everyone hates this step. Sparing the extras feels kind and is not: crowded seedlings starve each other into weakness, all of them. One strong plant per container is the goal. Snip, do not mourn. ## Feeding, briefly Seed-starting mix contains little or no food, but a seed carries its own lunchbox, so nothing is needed at first. Once a seedling has several sets of "true leaves" (the adult-shaped leaves that appear after the first plain pair), feed weekly with a water-soluble fertilizer mixed at one quarter of the package strength. Full-strength fertilizer burns seedlings. If your bag is a potting mix with fertilizer already in it, it can carry a seedling for at least 6 weeks with no additions. ## Damping-off: the classic seedling killer Damping-off is a group of soil-dwelling molds and fungi that attack seeds and new seedlings. You will know it when you see it: seeds that never come up, or seedlings that looked fine yesterday now collapsed flat, the stem pinched, brown, and water-soaked at the soil line. Sometimes a fluffy white cobweb growth appears on the mix. There is no cure once a seedling falls; prevention is the whole game: - Use new, bagged seed-starting or potting mix, never garden soil, compost, or last year's mix. - Sterilize previously used pots and trays: soak 30 minutes in a 10% bleach solution (1 part plain household bleach to 9 parts water), then rinse well. Handle with care: this solution is for tools only, never for drinking or skin contact, keep it away from children and pets, mix it in a ventilated space, and never combine bleach with other cleaners. - Water with clean, room-temperature water, and never let containers sit soggy; water from below and pour off the excess. - Keep germination warm (the 70 to 75 F mat) so seedlings sprint through their vulnerable stage, and give sprouted seedlings their full 12 to 16 hours of light. - Gentle air movement from a small fan on low, out of splash range of the watering tray, helps the surface dry between waterings. ## Hardening off: the two-week goodbye An indoor seedling has never met wind, direct sun, or a cold night; put it straight into the garden and it scalds and stalls. "Hardening off" is a one-to-two-week transition that toughens it up. Beginning about two weeks before transplant day: 1. Days 1 and 2: set the plants outside in a shaded, wind-protected spot for a few hours (two or three) on a mild day, then bring them back in. 2. Each following day: leave them out a little longer and let them have a little more direct sun, morning sun first. 3. Bring them in every night, and skip any day that is windy or below 45 F; cold and wind undo the work. 4. Water a bit less during these weeks (never to the point of wilting); slight thirst also toughens. 5. By the end of the transition they can stand a full day of sun and are ready for the ground. ## Transplant timing Cool-season crops (broccoli, cabbage, lettuce) can go out a few weeks before the last frost date. Warm-season crops (tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, squash) wait until all danger of frost is past and the soil has warmed; their roots grow poorly in cold soil, and frost kills them outright. Watch the forecast, not just the calendar: the frost date is an average, and one cold night can erase two months of work. If frost threatens after transplanting, cover the plants overnight. ## What can go wrong - Nothing germinated: usually one of four causes. Too cold (the mix, not the room, must reach the 65 to 75 F range); planted too deep (the twice-the-seed's-width rule); moisture failure (the mix dried out mid-sprout, or stayed so wet the seeds rotted); or old, dead seed. Check the packet's days-to-germinate before declaring failure, add warmth, and resow shallower. Two weeks and a resow is all a total loss costs. - Mold or green film on the soil surface: the surface is staying wet and the air is still. Water less often, always from below, pour off standing water, and add the small fan. Surface mold is a warning shot, not yet a dead tray; damping-off follows the same conditions. - Leggy, pale seedlings: not enough light, full stop. Move the light down to a few inches above the leaves, run it 12 to 16 hours, and cooler days will help. Leggy tomato seedlings get one mercy: at transplant time, bury the extra stem, and it grows roots. - Seedlings collapsed at the base: that is damping-off (see above). Remove the fallen and their containers from the tray, let the survivors' surface dry, add air movement, and review the prevention list; next sowing, start with clean everything. ## How you know it worked Stout, short-stemmed seedlings with deep green true leaves, standing straight without leaning; roots that hold the mix together in one piece when you slide a plant out; and after hardening off, plants that shrug off a full day outdoors. If, some weeks after transplant, you are eating from a plant that existed only as a dry speck in an envelope last winter, you have the whole skill, and every packet on the seed rack is now an open door. ## Sources University extension services (Minnesota, Maryland) and one garden education nonprofit (retail price ballparks): - https://extension.umn.edu/planting-and-growing-guides/starting-seeds-indoors - https://extension.umn.edu/solve-problem/how-prevent-seedling-damping - https://extension.umd.edu/resource/starting-vegetable-seeds-indoors - https://extension.umd.edu/resource/when-plant-vegetables - https://extension.umd.edu/resource/hardening-vegetable-seedlings-home-garden - https://www.civicgardencenter.org/blog/should-i-get-transplants-or-grow-from-seed

headings: Rule 2: start with plants that pollinate themselves
Choosing which plants to save from
The germination test: ten minutes, all doubt removed
docs.text: # Saving Your Own Seeds A seed you saved yourself cannot be discontinued, cannot be recalled, and cannot be priced out of your reach. That is the whole point of this skill. Everything else in a garden can be bought; the seed is the one part that can also be made, by you, out of a plant you already grew. Do it once and you stop being only a customer of the food system and become a small node inside it. This guide is the companion to Starting Seeds. That guide is about sowing a seed someone else produced. This one is about producing the seed. Save your own, start them with that guide next spring, and the loop closes. One honest thing first: seed saving has two ways to fail that you will not discover for a full year. Save from the wrong kind of plant, or let the wrong plants breed together, and the seed looks perfect, sprouts perfectly, and grows into something you did not want. Both failures are avoidable, and both are explained below, but neither shows up until the following season. Read the two rules before you save anything. ## Rule 1: open-pollinated, never hybrid Look at the seed packet or the plant label. If it says **hybrid** or **F1**, do not save seed from it. A hybrid is a deliberate cross between two different parent lines. The plant itself is often excellent. Its seed is not. The University of Maine puts it plainly: F1 hybrids are not true-breeding, and their seed "will produce a population of plants displaying traits covering the full genetic range." Minnesota Extension gives the everyday version, using 'Big Boy' and 'Early Girl' tomatoes as the example. The seeds are alive and will grow, but "plants grown from that seed are not identical to the hybrid parents." What you want instead is **open-pollinated**, which includes everything sold as **heirloom**. Minnesota's wording: open-pollinated varieties "will come true from seed," producing nearly identical fruit. If the packet does not say either way, assume hybrid. Open-pollinated is a selling point, and seed companies print it. This rule costs you nothing to obey. Next spring, buy open-pollinated packets of the crops you intend to save, and buy hybrids only for crops you are content to re-buy forever. ## Rule 2: start with plants that pollinate themselves Some plants fertilize their own flowers before anything else can reach them. Their seed comes out like the parent even when another variety is growing a few feet away. Others are pollinated by insects or by wind, which means a bee or a gust chose the other parent, and you find out next August. **Start here (self-pollinating, easy):** beans, peas, tomatoes, lettuce. Those four are on the University of Maine's self-pollinated list, and Minnesota names tomatoes, beans and peas as good choices, with "seeds that require little or no special treatment before storage." **Peppers: the sources disagree, so treat them as insect-pollinated.** Minnesota lists peppers among its beginner crops, but Maine's table puts pepper and eggplant in the insect-pollinated column, not the self-pollinated one. Follow Maine here, because the failure mode is specific and unpleasant: bees cross a sweet pepper with a hot one, and you discover the capsaicin next August in what you believed was a bell pepper. Grow only one pepper variety in any season you intend to save seed from. **Insect-pollinated (harder):** peppers, eggplant, squash, pumpkins, melons, cucumbers, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, carrots, radish. **Wind-pollinated (hardest):** corn, beets, Swiss chard. Four crops is not a limitation, it is a curriculum. Beans, peas, lettuce and tomatoes give you a protein crop, a cool-season crop, a salad crop, and the fruit almost everybody starts with. Learn on those. ## The traps, named **Hybrids.** Covered above. The most common disappointment there is. **Biennials.** Some crops we eat in their first year do not flower and make seed until their second. Carrots, beets, onions, parsnips, cabbage and their relatives are biennial, so saving their seed takes two growing seasons. In a cold climate it also means digging the roots in autumn and, as Maine Extension describes, storing them at or near freezing until spring so you can replant them. Minnesota simply notes that these "are harder to save since the plants need two growing seasons to set seed." None of this is impossible. It is a different and longer project, and it does not belong in your first year. **Squash and its relatives.** This is the trap that produces the famous inedible mystery squash. South Dakota State University Extension groups them by which will cross with which: - Group one, all of which cross with each other: zucchini, yellow crookneck, acorn, spaghetti, patty pan, delicata, pumpkins and gourds. - Group two, which cross with each other: butternut, buttercup, banana, Hubbard and turban squashes. - Group three, which cross with each other but not with squashes, pumpkins or cucumbers: muskmelon, cantaloupe, Charentais, honeydew, casaba, Armenian cucumber, snake melon. - Cucumbers, watermelon and loofah gourds cross only within their own kind, so they matter only if you grow two varieties of the same one. To keep a variety pure, SDSU says these need to be separated by "one-half to one mile," which no home garden has. Buildings, a thick stand of trees or a hill in between will shorten that, but the reliable home answers are simpler: grow only one variety from each group in a season, or hand-pollinate. To hand-pollinate, in early morning move pollen from a male flower to a female flower with a small paintbrush, do it within four hours of the female flower opening, and bag or tape the flower closed again afterward. **Corn.** Wind carries corn pollen a long way. Minnesota's example is the one to remember: "popcorn can pollinate a stand of sweet corn from a nearby garden on a windy day," which ruins both. Corn is not a beginner's seed-saving crop in a neighborhood. ## Choosing which plants to save from You are not only collecting seed, you are choosing the parents of next year's garden. So choose on purpose: - Save from plants that stayed healthy all season. Never save from a diseased plant; some diseases travel on the seed. - Save from plants that looked and tasted the way the variety is supposed to. If one bean plant matured three weeks before all the others, that is either a plant worth keeping or a stray from a different variety, and you have to decide which. - Save from several plants, not one. For the easy self-pollinating four, a handful is plenty. For anything cross-pollinated, SDSU suggests saving from 5 to 10 plants to keep a variety healthy, and 25 plants for a rare variety you are trying to preserve. - Let the seed crop stay on the plant far longer than the eating crop. Those plants are finished as food. They are seed factories now. ## Dry seeds: beans, peas, lettuce These are the simplest. The seed dries on the plant and you collect it. 1. Stop harvesting from a few chosen plants and let their pods stay on. Minnesota's finish line for beans and peas: leave the pods until "they are dry and start to turn brown, with the seeds rattling inside," which "may take as long as a month after you would normally harvest." 2. If a frost or a week of rain is coming, pull the whole plant and hang it somewhere dry and airy to finish. 3. Bring the pods indoors and dry them further before you open them. Minnesota says at least two weeks before shelling. 4. Shell the seed out. Maine describes the traditional way to do a large batch: put the dry pods in a sack and thresh them by crushing or treading, then winnow, which means pouring the mix from one bowl to another in front of a fan so the light chaff blows sideways and the heavy seed falls straight down. Lettuce works the same way but looks different. Let the plant bolt, which means send up a flower stalk, let the flowers turn into small dandelion-style puffs, and collect the puffs as they dry. Lettuce ripens over weeks rather than all at once, so plan on several passes. ## Wet seeds: tomatoes Tomato seeds arrive wrapped in a jelly that stops them sprouting inside the fruit, so they get a short deliberate ferment that removes it. It smells bad for a few days. That is normal. 1. Pick fully ripe, healthy fruit from a plant that stayed healthy. 2. Scoop the seeds and jelly into a jar and add water. 3. Leave it at room temperature and, in Minnesota's instruction, "stir or swirl the mixture twice a day. The mixture will ferment and the seeds should sink to the bottom within five days." 4. Pour off the floating pulp and the floating seeds. Maine's rule is that the "strong, viable seeds will sink to the bottom," so the floaters are the ones to discard. Rinse with clean water repeatedly until only clean seed is left. 5. Spread the seed in a single layer to dry. Maine notes that tomato seeds stick badly to paper towels and that coffee filters work better, and that you should shake them loose several times a day. Peppers need none of this. Minnesota: leave some fruit on the plant "until they become fully ripe and start to wrinkle," then remove the seeds and spread them out to dry. Wear gloves for hot peppers and keep your hands away from your eyes. ## Drying: the step people rush Wet seed rots or molds in the jar. This is the most common way a carefully saved harvest is lost after all the real work is finished. Colorado State University Extension is clearest on the target: "the drier the seeds, the longer they will store," and seed should be dried "to less than 8 percent moisture." Their method for finishing a batch is to dry seed at 100 degrees F for six hours. Do not use a microwave, and if you use an oven, keep it at its lowest setting with the door propped open so it never exceeds 100 F. Maine adds the ceiling that matters if you are drying in a warm room or a sunny window: the temperature must not exceed 96 F, and keep seed out of direct sun. For most home savers, a week or two spread on a plate or a screen in a dry, airy, shaded indoor spot does the job. A bean seed is dry enough when it shatters rather than dents under a hammer tap, and when you cannot mark it with a fingernail. ## Storing: cool, dry, dark, labeled Two things decide how long seed lives: how dry it is, and how cold it is. - **Container.** Colorado State says use "sealed cans or jars, rather than plastic bags," because those are genuinely moisture-proof. Minnesota says tightly sealed glass containers. A canning jar with a fresh lid is ideal and is probably already in the house. - **Temperature.** Minnesota says store between 32 and 41 F, which in practice means a refrigerator. Colorado says keep the temperature below 40 F, and a freezer also works for thoroughly dried seed. - **Humidity.** Colorado gives the numbers. At 15 percent relative humidity, seed settles at about 6 percent moisture and "will store safely in this condition for several years." At 90 percent humidity it reaches 19 percent moisture and "germination will be poor after one year." A rule of thumb used widely in the seed trade: the storage temperature in degrees Fahrenheit plus the relative humidity in percent should add up to less than 100. - **A drying agent, if your air is damp.** Minnesota suggests one to two tablespoons of silica gel, or powdered milk from a freshly opened package, wrapped in paper at the bottom of the jar. Powdered milk keeps absorbing moisture for about six months, then needs replacing. - **Label everything** with the crop, the variety, and the date you collected it. You will not remember. Nobody remembers. ## How long saved seed lasts Two extension services publish longevity tables, and they do not fully agree. That disagreement is itself worth knowing about. University of Maine, expected storage life in years: - **1 to 2 years:** onion, parsnip, sweet corn - **3 years:** bean, carrot, leek, pea - **4 years:** beet, pepper, pumpkin, tomato - **5 years:** Brussels sprouts, cabbage, cauliflower, cucumber, lettuce, melon, radish, squash, watermelon Colorado State's table gives lettuce 1 year and onion 1 year, with beans 3, peas 3, carrot 3, tomato 4, squash 4, and sweet corn 2. So Maine says lettuce keeps five years and Colorado says one. Both are real extension guidance. The gap is mostly about how well the seed was dried and how cold it was kept, which is exactly what you control. The honest way to use these tables: plan on the shorter number, and settle the question with a germination test rather than an argument. Minnesota takes the most conservative line of all and simply advises using saved seed within one year, because "the older the seed the lower the germination and vigor." ## The germination test: ten minutes, all doubt removed Do this in late winter, before you commit a season to seed that may be dead. Maine's method: 1. Count out 25 seeds of a large-seeded crop, or up to 100 of a small-seeded one. 2. Space them on a dampened paper towel, roll it up, and seal the roll in a plastic bag. 3. Leave it somewhere warm for 7 days. 4. Unroll it and count how many sprouted. Twenty out of 25 is 80 percent, which is fine; sow normally. Ten out of 25 is 40 percent, which is still usable if you sow twice as thickly. Two out of 25 means buy fresh seed, and be glad you found out in February instead of June. ## A note on seed-borne disease Some plant diseases ride on the outside of a seed into next year's garden. If you have had disease problems, Minnesota publishes two treatments: - A bleach soak: one part household bleach at 5.25 percent sodium hypochlorite to four parts water, with a drop of soap. Soak the seed for one minute, then rinse for 5 minutes. - A hot water treatment, for tomato seed only: warm at 100 F for 10 minutes, then hold at 122 F for 25 minutes, then rinse for 5 minutes. Both are precise for a reason. The hot water treatment needs a real thermometer, because a few degrees hotter kills the seed and a few degrees cooler accomplishes nothing. The bleach solution is for seed, never for skin and never for drinking. Mix it with ventilation, keep it away from children and pets, and never combine bleach with other cleaners. ## What can go wrong - **Everything came out wrong the following year.** Almost always the hybrid rule. Check the packet you saved from. If it says F1, that is the answer, and nothing you did in the harvesting or drying was at fault. - **The squash is a stranger.** Two varieties from the same crossing group flowered near each other. The fruit is usually still safe to eat and is occasionally good, but the variety is gone. Next year grow one variety per group, or hand-pollinate. - **Mold in the jar.** The seed was not dry enough, or the jar went into a warm humid cupboard. Discard moldy seed. Next time dry it longer, add a drying agent, and store it cold. - **Nothing germinated in the test.** Either the seed was harvested before it was mature, since green, soft, pale seed is not finished seed, or it was dried too hot. Both are common first-attempt mistakes. - **The lettuce fluff blew away.** It does. Cut the whole seed stalk into a paper bag and let it finish drying in there. - **You saved from the first plant to bolt.** For lettuce and the cabbage family, early bolting is the single trait you least want to breed for. Save from the last plants to bolt, not the first. ## How you know it worked - Your jar holds clean, hard, fully dry seed, labeled with crop, variety and date, sitting somewhere cold and dark. - A germination test in late winter comes back above roughly 70 percent. - Next season, the plants that come up look like the plants you saved them from. At that point something quiet and permanent has happened. You no longer depend on anyone's catalog to grow that crop again. The garden that fed you also reproduced itself, and it will keep doing that for as long as you keep choosing good parents. ## Sources University extension services (Minnesota, Maine, Colorado State, South Dakota State): - https://extension.umn.edu/planting-and-growing-guides/saving-vegetable-seeds - https://extension.umaine.edu/publications/2750e/ - https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/storing-vegetable-and-flower-seeds/ - https://extension.sdstate.edu/saving-seed-pumpkins-squash-cucumbers-melons-and-gourds

docs.title: Growing Food You Can Live On
headings: Growing Food You Can Live On
docs.text: # Growing Food You Can Live On A tomato is a wonderful first success and a nutritionally minor one. Here is the number that makes the point. Using USDA food composition data, a pound of raw tomatoes holds about 82 calories. A pound of potatoes holds about 350. A pound of dry beans holds about 1,550. You cannot live on tomatoes. That is not a criticism of the tomato, and Your First Tomato is still the right place to begin, because a first success teaches watering, light and patience faster than any reading does. But if the ambition is to feed yourself rather than to garnish a meal, the crops change, the arithmetic changes, and the honest numbers are worth seeing before you plan a garden around them. This guide covers the three crops that carry a beginner furthest: **potatoes** for calories, **dry beans** for protein and long storage, and **winter squash** for calories that keep for months without electricity. They are chosen because each one is forgiving, each one stores without a freezer, and together they are the classic backbone of a subsistence garden in most of the temperate world. One honest thing first, and it is a bigger one than usual: this guide tells you what a plot can produce, not what a person should eat. No three crops make a complete diet. Feeding yourself entirely from a garden is a serious nutritional project involving fats, vitamin B12, and much else, and it is a question for a dietitian, not for a garden guide. What follows is the scale, so you can see what a given piece of ground actually does. ## What the numbers actually say Every figure below comes from a university extension service or from USDA food composition data. The multiplication is ours and we show it, so you can check it or redo it with your own local figures. **Calorie density**, from USDA FoodData Central, per 100 grams raw. The conversion to pounds is ours, at 453.6 grams to the pound. - **Tomato**, red ripe, raw: 18 calories per 100 g, protein 0.9 g. Per pound, **about 82 calories**. - **Potato**, flesh and skin, raw: 77 calories per 100 g, protein 2.1 g. Per pound, **about 350 calories**. - **Winter squash**, butternut, raw: 45 calories per 100 g, protein 1.0 g. Per pound, **about 205 calories**. - **Dry beans**, black, mature seeds, raw: 341 calories per 100 g, protein 21.6 g. Per pound, **about 1,550 calories**. **Yield per 100 feet of row (extension figures):** - **Potatoes: 200 to 300 lb**, per Iowa State, whose figure is 20 to 30 lb per 10-foot row. - **Potatoes: 75 to 100 lb**, per Utah State. - **Dry beans: 20 to 25 lb**, per Utah State. - **Winter squash: 75 to 100 lb**, per Utah State. Look at the two potato figures. Two real extension services, both giving home-garden guidance, differ by a factor of three. That is not an error in either one. Iowa is deep prairie soil with a long humid summer; Utah is arid, high, and short-seasoned. Everything about garden yield depends on soil, water, season length, variety and how well the season goes, and a first-year garden on unimproved ground will land at the bottom of any published range or below it. So treat every yield figure you ever read, including these, as a planning estimate rather than a promise, and plan on the low number. **Putting them together (our arithmetic):** Calories from one 100-foot row, and how many days of one adult's food energy that is: - **Potatoes, Utah figure:** 26,000 to 35,000 calories, **13 to 18 days**. - **Potatoes, Iowa figure:** 70,000 to 105,000 calories, **35 to 53 days**. - **Dry beans:** 31,000 to 39,000 calories, **15 to 19 days**. - **Winter squash:** 15,000 to 20,000 calories, **8 to 10 days**. The days figures use 2,000 calories a day, which the FDA states is "used as a general guide for nutrition advice," while noting that your own needs "may be higher or lower and vary depending on your age, sex, height, weight, and physical activity level." A working adult doing physical labor needs more. Two cautions on those figures. The winter squash line is generous, because the yield figure is whole fruit and you do not eat the skin or the seed cavity, so the real number is lower. And the dry bean line understates what beans are for: their value is the 21.6 grams of protein in every 100 grams, which works out to roughly 4.3 to 5.4 pounds of protein from a 100-foot row, alongside a food that keeps for years in a jar. **How much ground is that?** Utah State spaces potato rows 30 to 36 inches apart and Iowa State says 2 to 3 feet, so a 100-foot potato row plus the walking space beside it occupies roughly 300 square feet. Bean rows at 18 to 24 inches occupy roughly 200 square feet per 100 feet of row. Winter squash is planted in mounds 4 feet apart, but the vines sprawl well past the row, so its real footprint is considerably larger than the row length suggests. Do not scale these figures up across a whole plot as though the whole plot were productive row; a real garden loses ground to paths, edges, shade and the corner where nothing grows. ## Potatoes: the calorie crop Potatoes produce more food energy per square foot than almost anything else a beginner can grow, they store for months without a freezer, and they are grown from pieces of potato rather than from seed. **Planting.** Utah State: plant 2 to 3 weeks before your last frost date, once soils are at least 50 F. Buy certified seed potatoes rather than using supermarket potatoes, which are often treated to suppress sprouting. Cut them so each piece weighs at least 2 ounces and has one or more eyes, the small dimples that sprout. You need 8 to 10 pounds of seed potatoes for every 100 feet of row. Seed potatoes are frequently treated with fungicide before sale, so plant them, do not eat them, and keep them away from the kitchen and out of reach of children. **Spacing.** Utah State: 4 to 6 inches deep, 10 to 12 inches apart in the row, rows 30 to 36 inches apart. Iowa State's version is a furrow 4 inches deep with pieces about 1 foot apart and rows 2 to 3 feet apart. Either works. **Growing.** Iowa State: at least six hours of direct sun each day, 1 inch of water per week through the season, and 1 to 2 pounds of all-purpose garden fertilizer such as 10-10-10 per 100 square feet. Keep cultivation shallow, 2 inches or less, because the tubers form near the surface and a deep hoe cuts them. Pull soil up around the stems as they grow, which is called hilling, so developing potatoes stay covered. **Harvest.** Iowa State: 90 to 120 days after planting for a full crop. You can steal a few new potatoes earlier once they are more than an inch and a half across, but use those within ten days; they have no skin to speak of and will not store. **Curing and storage.** Utah State: cure the tubers at 55 to 60 F with high humidity for 2 to 3 weeks after harvest, then store in the dark at 40 to 45 F through the winter. Iowa State's long-term figure is 40 F at 90 percent relative humidity, with a two-week cure at 50 to 60 F and 85 to 90 percent humidity first. Do not store potatoes with apples or other fruit, which give off a ripening gas that shortens their storage life. **The one real safety rule.** Potatoes exposed to light turn green and produce solanine, a natural toxin. Utah State: the chemical "tastes bitter after being cooked," and you should "discard very green tubers." Cut away small green patches generously; throw out badly greened potatoes. Store them in the dark, always. This is also why potato leaves and fruits are not food; the plant is in the nightshade family and only the tuber is edible. ## Dry beans: the protein crop A dry bean is the same plant as a green bean, left on the vine until the seed inside the pod is fully mature and hard. That one change turns a perishable vegetable into a food that stores for years at room temperature in a jar, and it is the single easiest protein a beginner can produce. **Planting.** Utah State: about 3 to 4 ounces of seed plants 100 feet of row. Sow 1 inch deep, 2 to 3 inches apart, in rows 18 to 24 inches apart. Beans need soil and air temperatures above 60 F; they rot in cold wet ground and they will not take a frost at either end of the season. **Timing matters more than for most crops.** Dry beans must stay on the plant to the very end of the season, so they need the whole season. Utah State's warning is worth taking seriously: dry beans planted after July 1 "generally will not mature in cooler areas of Utah but will produce mature seeds in the warmer regions of Southern Utah." Translate that to where you live by counting the frost-free days you get and comparing them to the days-to-maturity on the packet, with a few weeks of margin. If the margin is thin, choose the earliest variety you can find. Unlike snap beans, there is no picking through the summer. The whole crop comes in at once. **Harvest and drying.** Utah State: "Pull up the plants and lay in a row in the garden for 5 to 7 days. Once plants are dry, remove the pods, shell out the seeds and allow some additional time for the seeds to dry further." If rain is forecast during those days, move the plants under cover; a soaked, half-dried bean crop molds. **Storage.** Sealed containers in a cool dry place. Beans that are properly dry rattle hard and cannot be dented with a fingernail. **Dry beans must be fully cooked.** This is a real safety rule, not a matter of taste. Raw and undercooked dry beans contain a natural toxin called phytohaemagglutinin. The FDA's Bad Bug Book records that red kidney beans carry the most of it, and that as few as four or five improperly cooked red kidney beans can cause severe vomiting within a few hours, followed by diarrhea. Kansas State University Extension gives the procedure: soak the beans for at least five hours, drain and discard the soaking water, then boil in fresh water for at least 30 minutes. The toxin breaks down at boiling temperature in about 10 minutes, and the longer 30 minutes is the margin researchers advise. And the counterintuitive part: **do not cook dry beans in a slow cooker.** K-State's wording is blunt: "Don't use a slow cooker: it likely won't get hot enough." A slow cooker held below boiling can leave the toxin intact while making the beans soft enough to eat, which is how most poisonings happen. Boil first on the stove, then move them to the slow cooker if you want to. Canned beans from a store are already cooked and are not affected by any of this. **A bonus.** Dry beans are self-pollinating, which makes them one of the best crops to save your own seed from. See Saving Your Own Seeds. Once you grow an open-pollinated dry bean, you never need to buy that seed again. ## Winter squash: the storage crop Winter squash is not a variety of squash so much as a moment of harvest. It is left on the vine until the rind hardens into armor, and that armor is why it keeps for months in an unheated room with no processing at all. It costs you space, not effort. **Planting.** Utah State: plant 4 to 6 seeds in mounds 4 feet apart, 1 to 2 inches deep, once soils reach 65 F. After the seedlings have two leaves, thin to two plants per mound. **Harvest.** Utah State: squash are mature "when fruits are fully colored, when vines begin to die back, and when the rind is hard and impervious to scratching from a fingernail." Iowa State adds that mature squash have dull rather than glossy surfaces. Cut, do not pull, and leave about a 1-inch stem on each fruit; a squash that loses its stem rots at the scar. Bring them all in before a hard frost. **Curing.** Iowa State: cure winter squash, except acorn types, at 80 to 85 F and 80 to 85 percent relative humidity. Do not cure acorn squash. Curing hardens the skin and heals small scratches, and it is the difference between a squash that keeps and one that goes soft in November. **Storage.** Iowa State: a cool, dry, well-ventilated place at 50 to 55 F. Not the fridge, and not near apples or pears, which give off ripening gas that shortens storage. How long they keep depends entirely on type: Iowa State gives acorn about 5 to 8 weeks, butternut 2 to 3 months, and Hubbard 5 to 6 months. Utah State agrees on the pattern, noting that buttercup and banana squash store longer than butternut and acorn. If you want food in February, those storage numbers are the whole decision. Grow the long-keeping types. ## The honest counterweight Set the guides side by side. Your First Tomato is a container, six hours of sun, one plant, and a season that ends with something delicious that holds roughly 82 calories a pound. This guide is rows, a real plot, months of storage, and food that holds four to nineteen times as much energy per pound. Both are real gardening. The difference is that the first one teaches you to garden and the second one starts to feed you, and it would be dishonest to let the first stand in for the second. A garden that produces salad is a hobby with benefits. A garden that produces a winter's worth of potatoes, beans and squash is the beginning of not needing permission to eat. It is also, plainly, more work and more ground. A 100-foot row is not a balcony. If you have only a balcony, grow the tomato and the herbs, and use this guide as the map for the day you have soil, or as the reason to go looking for a community garden plot. ## What can go wrong - **The yield came in far under the published figures.** Expected, especially in year one. The published figures assume decent soil, adequate water and a full season. Improve the soil (see Your First Compost), water more consistently, and compare next year, which is the only comparison that means anything. - **Potatoes came out small and few.** Usually not enough water during the weeks when tubers are forming, or not enough sun, or the plants were crowded. Potatoes are thirsty; the 1 inch a week is not optional. - **Potatoes green in storage.** Light got in. Store them in the dark, in a box or a paper sack, and discard badly greened tubers. - **The dry beans never dried.** The season ended first. Either the variety needed more days than you have, or planting was too late. Next year plant at the earliest safe date with the earliest variety you can find. Beans caught by frost while still green are not wasted; shell and eat them fresh as shell beans. - **Beans molded on the drying plants.** Rain during the field-drying days. Move plants under cover next time. - **Winter squash went soft by November.** Either it was picked immature, or it lost its stem, or it was not cured, or it was stored too warm or next to fruit. Check those four in that order. - **Vines took over the garden.** They do. Winter squash is a land animal. Plant it at the edge where it can sprawl outward, or grow a bush variety, or plan for it next year. ## How you know it worked - You harvested a crop you had to find somewhere to store, rather than eat that week. - Potatoes are in the dark at around 40 F, dry beans are in sealed jars, and cured squash is on a shelf at around 50 F. - In February you cook a meal whose main ingredient you grew in July. That last one is the real threshold. Growing food in season is pleasant. Eating in winter from ground you tended in summer is a different capability, and it is the one that makes a household harder to squeeze. Next: Keeping What You Grew covers drying, freezing, root cellaring and canning, which is how the rest of the harvest joins these three in lasting. And Saving Your Own Seeds closes the loop, so next year's crop does not begin with a purchase. ## Sources University extension services (Iowa State, Utah State, Kansas State), USDA FoodData Central, and the US Food and Drug Administration: - https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/how-to/growing-potatoes-home-garden - https://extension.usu.edu/yardandgarden/research/potatoes-in-the-garden - https://extension.usu.edu/yardandgarden/research/beans-in-the-garden - https://extension.usu.edu/yardandgarden/research/summer-and-winter-squash-in-the-garden - https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/faq/what-proper-way-harvest-and-store-winter-squash - https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/how-to/storing-winter-storage-vegetables - https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/ (FoodData Central; entries used: potatoes flesh and skin raw 170026, beans black mature seeds raw 173734, squash winter butternut raw 169295, tomatoes red ripe raw year round average 170457) - https://www.fda.gov/food/nutrition-facts-label/how-understand-and-use-nutrition-facts-label - https://www.fda.gov/files/food/published/Bad-Bug-Book-2nd-Edition-(PDF).pdf (FDA Bad Bug Book, phytohaemagglutinin) - https://enewsletters.k-state.edu/youaskedit/2017/10/13/cooking-dry-beans-safely/

docs.title: Keeping What You Grew
headings: The one rule that everything else hangs on
Method 3: Root cellaring (the one that costs nothing)
Method 4: Water-bath canning, acid foods only
A complete tested procedure: crushed tomatoes
docs.text: # Keeping What You Grew A garden does not hand you food evenly. It hands you nothing for months and then, over about three weeks, more than you can eat. Preserving is what turns that spike into a supply, and it is the difference between a garden that decorates your summer and a garden that feeds your winter. There are four methods worth a beginner's time, and they are not interchangeable. Drying and freezing are easy and forgiving. Root cellaring is nearly free and requires only the right corner of a building. Canning is the one with real stakes. **Read this before anything else.** Home canning done wrong can kill people. The organism is *Clostridium botulinum*, and the poison it makes cannot be seen, smelled or tasted. The National Center for Home Food Preservation, which publishes the USDA's tested procedures, states it without cushioning: "Even a taste of food containing this toxin can be fatal." That risk is entirely manageable, because it is entirely understood. It is managed by following tested procedures exactly and by never improvising one. This guide gives you the safety architecture, one complete tested canning procedure, and clear boundaries around everything it does not teach. Where a method is outside its scope, it says so and points you to where the real instructions live, rather than teaching you half of it. ## The one rule that everything else hangs on Some foods are acidic enough that *C. botulinum* cannot grow in them. Everything else is not, and requires far more heat to make safe. NCHFP draws the line at **pH 4.6**. Acid foods have a pH of 4.6 or lower; low-acid foods are above it. - **Acid foods**, in NCHFP's list: "Fruits, pickles, sauerkraut, jams, jellies, marmalades, and fruit butters." - **Low-acid foods**, in NCHFP's list: "Red meats, seafood, poultry, milk, and all fresh vegetables except for most tomatoes." Read that second list again. **All fresh vegetables.** Green beans, corn, carrots, potatoes, peas, squash, beets, greens. Every one of them is low-acid. Now the heat. A boiling water canner reaches the temperature of boiling water, 212 F at sea level, and no higher; that is a physical ceiling, not a matter of boiling longer. A pressure canner reaches 240 to 250 F, operating at 10 to 15 pounds of pressure. NCHFP: "Botulinum spores are very hard to destroy at boiling-water temperatures; the higher the canner temperature, the more easily they are destroyed." Which produces the rule: > **Low-acid foods CANNOT be safely canned in a boiling water bath.** > **They require a pressure canner.** NCHFP: "Pressure canning is the only > recommended method for canning meat, poultry, seafood, and vegetables," > and "using boiling water canners for these foods poses a real risk of > botulism poisoning." Green beans, corn, carrots and meat in a water-bath canner are not a shortcut and not an old family tradition worth continuing. They are the classic route to botulism. A sealed jar is exactly the low-oxygen environment the organism wants: NCHFP lists its growth conditions as a moist low-acid food, a temperature between 40 and 120 F, and less than 2 percent oxygen. A sealed jar of green beans on a shelf is all three. **This guide does not teach pressure canning.** Pressure canning is safe, well documented, and genuinely worth learning, but it needs specific equipment, gauge testing, and a tested time and pressure for every single food, and it is not something to learn from a general article. Learn it from the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning or from NCHFP directly, both linked in Sources, or from a class at your local extension office. Note also that NCHFP does not support using USDA canning processes in electric multicookers, even models with a "canning" button, because the processes were developed and tested for stovetop pressure canners. ## Method 1: Freezing (easiest, start here) Freezing keeps quality better than any other home method, and unlike canning it introduces no hazard of its own. What it does not do is kill anything. Freezing pauses spoilage; it does not sterilize. Food that was questionable going in is questionable coming out, and it starts spoiling again the moment it thaws, which is why frozen food is thawed in the refrigerator or under cold running water and not left out on the counter. **Temperature.** Colorado State University Extension: 0 degrees F or lower. A freezer compartment inside a refrigerator often runs warmer than that, which is why food stored there declines faster. **Blanching, and why it is not optional.** Vegetables carry enzymes that kept them growing, and those enzymes keep working in the freezer. CSU: after maturity, they "cause loss of quality, flavor, color, texture, and nutrients." Blanching, a brief scald, "slows or stops the enzyme action." Skip it and your green beans turn khaki and tasteless by January. CSU's method: 1. **Boiling water blanch:** at least 1 gallon of rapidly boiling water in a covered kettle. "Start counting time as soon as the vegetables are in the boiling water." 2. **Or steam blanch:** 1 to 2 inches of boiling water, vegetables held at least 3 inches above the bottom of the kettle. "Start counting steaming time as soon as the lid is on." 3. **Cool immediately.** Plunge the basket straight into a large quantity of cold water at 60 F or below, using about 1 pound of ice for each pound of vegetables. Cooling matters as much as the scald; vegetables left to cool slowly keep cooking. 4. **Drain, pack, freeze.** Times are per vegetable and per method, and they are short. CSU's examples: green beans 4 minutes in water; broccoli 4 minutes in water or 6 in steam; diced carrots 3 minutes in water. **Read that table's own footnote before you use those numbers.** It is a good lesson in where a published figure comes from. Colorado State notes that its "blanching times given are for 5,000 feet or higher. At altitudes below 5000 feet, subtract one minute from times given." Colorado is a high-altitude state and wrote its table for its own readers. Most of the world is below 5,000 feet, so for most readers those three examples are 3 minutes, 3 minutes (5 steaming), and 2 minutes. Get the full list from the CSU page in Sources, or from your own extension service, and check whose altitude a table was written for. Guessing a blanching time costs you quality rather than safety, but there is no reason to guess. **Packing.** CSU: leave 1/2 inch headspace at the top of rigid containers so the food can expand, and fill freezer bags to within 3 inches of the top. Press the air out of bags; air is what causes freezer burn. **How long.** CSU: "Most vegetables maintain high quality for 12 to 18 months at 0 degrees F or lower." That is a quality window, not a safety deadline. Food held continuously at 0 F stays safe indefinitely; it just stops being nice to eat. **The honest limitation.** Freezing depends on the power staying on. A freezer full of the year's harvest is a single point of failure, which is exactly why the other three methods in this guide exist. ## Method 2: Drying Drying removes the water that spoilage organisms need. It stores at room temperature, takes almost no space, and needs no power once the food is dry. **Temperature.** Penn State Extension: start at 145 F "when there is surface moisture on the fruit or vegetable," then "reduce the temperature to 135 to 140 F to finish drying." Starting hot while the surface is wet is safe because evaporation keeps the food itself cool; keeping it hot after that cooks the outside shut and traps moisture inside, a failure called case hardening, and food that is still damp in the middle will mold in the jar. **Equipment.** A food dehydrator is the straightforward answer. An oven works only if yours will genuinely hold a low temperature: Penn State says you need to set it to 140 to 150 F and prop the door open 2 to 3 inches. Many ovens will not go that low. **Sun drying is region-dependent.** It is a good example of why you should look up local guidance rather than trust any single article. Penn State says outright that "the high humidity in Pennsylvania makes this method impractical here." In a hot dry climate it is a traditional and effective method. The variable is your humidity, not your intent. **Knowing when it is done.** Penn State: fruit is done when it is "pliable and no beads of moisture form when pressed between your fingers." Vegetables are done when "tough, brittle, or crunchy." Test a piece after it has cooled, because warm food always feels softer. **Conditioning.** Pieces never dry evenly. Penn State: pack the cooled dried fruit loosely into an airtight glass or plastic container for several days so the remaining moisture spreads out evenly. Check daily. If you see condensation inside the jar, it is not dry enough; put it back in the dehydrator. **Insects.** Dried food from a home dryer can carry insect eggs. Penn State's treatment: heat in the oven at 160 F for 30 minutes, or freeze at 0 F or below for 48 hours, then store. **Storage.** Airtight, cool, dark. Cooler storage extends life substantially. ## Method 3: Root cellaring (the one that costs nothing) Some crops need no processing at all. They need the right corner. The insight worth carrying away is that there is no single set of "storage conditions"; there are three distinct climates, and putting a crop in the wrong one is why home storage usually fails. Iowa State University Extension's figures: - **Potatoes:** 40 F, 90 to 95 percent relative humidity, 5 to 8 months. - **Carrots:** 32 to 35 F, 98 to 100 percent humidity, 4 to 6 months. - **Beets:** 32 to 35 F, 95 percent humidity, 1 to 3 months. - **Onions:** 32 to 40 F, 65 to 70 percent humidity, 5 to 8 months. - **Winter squash:** 50 to 55 F, dry and well ventilated. Storage life by type: acorn 5 to 8 weeks, butternut 2 to 3 months, Hubbard 5 to 6 months. The three climates: - **Cold and very damp** for root crops. Carrots want humidity so high it is nearly condensing. Packed in damp sand or sawdust in a box is the traditional way to get there. - **Cold and dry** for onions and garlic. Same temperature as the roots, opposite humidity. They must not share a container with carrots. - **Cool and dry** for winter squash and pumpkins, notably warmer than the others. A refrigerator ruins winter squash. Two rules that apply throughout. Keep potatoes in the dark; light turns them green and bitter. And keep everything away from apples and pears, which give off a ripening gas that shortens storage life for potatoes and squash alike. Most homes have at least one of these climates somewhere: an unheated attached garage, a basement corner away from the furnace, an insulated crawl space, a spare room kept closed. Buy a cheap thermometer, put it where you are considering, and watch it for a week before you commit a harvest to it. ## Method 4: Water-bath canning, acid foods only Now the one with rules. Everything below applies **only** to acid foods: fruits, jams, jellies, pickles, sauerkraut, and tomatoes with acid added. Nothing else. Do not adapt it. ### Tomatoes and the acid problem Tomatoes sit right on the line, and they used to sit on the safe side of it. They no longer reliably do. As extension services now explain, newer varieties, over-mature fruit and tomatoes from frost-killed or dead vines can have a pH above 4.6, so tomatoes are no longer treated as acid foods, and the USDA requires acid to be added before processing. NCHFP's amounts, added directly to the jars before filling: - **Per pint jar:** 1 tablespoon bottled lemon juice, OR 1/4 teaspoon citric acid, OR 2 tablespoons of 5 percent vinegar. - **Per quart jar:** 2 tablespoons bottled lemon juice, OR 1/2 teaspoon citric acid, OR 4 tablespoons of 5 percent vinegar. NCHFP notes vinegar "may cause undesirable flavor changes." **It must be bottled lemon juice, not fresh.** This is not fussiness. Bottled lemon juice is standardized to a known acidity under FDA rules, while the acidity of a fresh lemon varies with variety, ripeness and growing conditions, and Iowa State Extension notes that fresh juice pH varies enough that you cannot rely on it for a safety margin. A lemon off your own tree is a lovely thing and it is not a measuring instrument. Never reduce the acid because the result tastes sharp. Add sugar if you must; the acid is not a seasoning. And note that acidification is required for tomatoes regardless of which canner you use. NCHFP is explicit that when a tomato procedure offers both a boiling water and a pressure option, every preparation step still applies, acidification included. Choosing the pressure canner does not excuse you from the lemon juice. **Use jars made for home canning.** NCHFP's procedures assume Mason-type canning jars with two-piece lids. Repurposed commercial food jars, mayonnaise jars and the like are not built for repeated heat cycling and break more often, sometimes during processing. ### A complete tested procedure: crushed tomatoes This is NCHFP's process, given in full so you can see what "tested procedure" means in practice. 1. Wash the tomatoes and dip them in boiling water for 30 to 60 seconds, or until the skins split. Dip in cold water, slip off the skins, and remove the cores. Trim any damaged areas and quarter them. 2. Heat about one-sixth of the pieces rapidly while crushing them to release juice. Add the rest, continuing to heat and stir until the whole pot is boiling, then keep it at a gentle boil for 5 minutes. 3. Add the bottled lemon juice or citric acid to each jar, in the amounts listed above. Optionally add 1 teaspoon of salt per quart. 4. Fill the jars immediately with the hot tomatoes, leaving 1/2 inch headspace. Wipe the rims, apply the lids. 5. Process in a boiling water canner for the time that matches your altitude: - 0 to 1,000 feet: pints 35 minutes, quarts 45 minutes. - 1,001 to 3,000 feet: pints 40 minutes, quarts 50 minutes. - 3,001 to 6,000 feet: pints 45 minutes, quarts 55 minutes. - Above 6,000 feet: pints 50 minutes, quarts 60 minutes. **Altitude is not optional.** Water boils cooler as you go up, so the same minutes deliver less heat. Look up your elevation once and write it inside your cupboard door. ### Running the canner NCHFP's boiling-water canner procedure: - Fill the canner about half full with clean warm water for a load of pints, and preheat the water to 140 F for raw-packed foods or 180 F for hot-packed foods. - Load the jars upright, using a jar lifter gripped below the neck. - Add boiling water until it stands at least 1 inch above the jar tops, or 2 inches above for any process longer than 30 minutes. Add more boiling water during processing if the level drops. - Start the timer only after the water is boiling, and time the full number of minutes. If the water stops boiling at any point, bring it back to a boil and start the timing over from the beginning. - When the time is up, turn off the heat and wait 5 minutes before removing jars, so the canner settles. - Set jars on a towel or a cooling rack with at least an inch between them, away from drafts and cold surfaces. - Leave them undisturbed for 12 to 24 hours. Do not tighten the ring bands and do not press the lid centers while they cool. - Remove the ring bands from sealed jars, label them, and store in a cool, dry, dark place. ### What not to do, ever - Do not water-bath any low-acid food. See the rule at the top. - Do not scale, halve, double or otherwise adjust a tested recipe. Processing times are tied to the exact contents and jar size tested. - Do not use a recipe without a tested source behind it. A recipe from social media, a blog, or a relative's notebook is not a tested process, however confident it sounds and however long it has been used without incident. Botulism is rare per jar, which is exactly why the anecdote "we always did it this way" is not evidence. - Do not can pureed or mashed vegetables. Pumpkin and winter squash are a standard example: NCHFP has a tested process for them cubed and pressure canned, and none for puree or butter, because in a dense puree there is no way to know the center of the jar reached temperature. No tested process means do not do it, not do it carefully. - Do not reuse the flat sealing lids. Rings are reusable; flats are not. ## When a jar goes wrong **Do not taste it.** NCHFP: "Do not taste food from a jar with an unsealed lid or food that shows signs of spoilage." Signs, in NCHFP's words: swelled lids and broken seals; "streaks of dried food originating at the top of the jar"; "rising air bubbles and unnatural color"; "cotton-like mold growth (white, blue, black, or green)"; unnatural odors; spurting liquid on opening. A jar can also be dangerous with no sign at all. That is the whole reason the procedures are strict. **Disposal, from NCHFP.** Wearing disposable rubber or heavy plastic gloves, place the suspect containers on their sides in an 8-quart or larger stock pot or boiling-water canner. Add water to cover them by at least 1 inch. Heat to boiling and boil 30 minutes. Then cool, and discard the containers, lids and food in the trash or at a landfill. **Cleanup.** NCHFP: use 1 part unscented liquid household chlorine bleach at 5 to 6 percent sodium hypochlorite to 5 parts clean water. Spray or wet the contaminated surfaces, let stand 30 minutes, repeat, then rinse thoroughly. Wash your hands afterward. Handle bleach in a ventilated space, keep it away from children and pets, and never mix it with other cleaners. **One more safety margin.** NCHFP: "Boiling food 10 minutes at elevations below 1,000 feet elevation should destroy this poison when it is present," and "for elevations at and above 1,000 feet, add 1 additional minute per 1,000 feet additional elevation." This is a sensible habit before serving home-canned low-acid food that was properly pressure canned. It is **not** a way to rescue food that was canned incorrectly, and it is not a reason to relax any rule above. Anything showing signs of spoilage gets the disposal procedure, not the stove. ## What can go wrong - **Jars did not seal.** Common causes: a chipped jar rim, food or acid left on the rim before the lid went on, a reused flat lid, headspace wrong, or the ring tightened too hard. An unsealed jar is not a disaster; refrigerate it and eat it within a few days, or freeze it. - **Liquid siphoned out during processing.** Usually the jars were cooled too fast or removed too soon. If the jar sealed, it is safe; it just looks poor. Wait the 5 minutes before removing jars next time. - **Frozen vegetables lost color and taste.** Blanching was skipped or cut short, or the freezer runs above 0 F. Check with a thermometer. - **Dried food molded in the jar.** It was not dry enough, or it was not conditioned. Redry the batch if you catch it early. Discard anything visibly moldy. - **Root-cellared carrots went limp.** Not humid enough. Pack in damp sand next time, or in perforated bags. - **Onions sprouted or rotted.** Too warm, or too humid because they were stored beside the roots. They need the cold dry corner. - **Potatoes turned green.** Light got in. Store them in the dark and discard badly greened tubers. ## How you know it worked - Every preserved item is labeled with what it is and the date. - Nothing you canned is a low-acid food in a water-bath jar. - Every canning recipe you used traces back to NCHFP, the USDA Complete Guide, or your extension service, without adjustments. - Your frozen food is at 0 F, your dried food shows no condensation inside the jar, and your stored roots, onions and squash are each in the climate the figures above say they want. - In February you open something you grew and it is good. ## The loop this closes Growing Food You Can Live On covers producing a real harvest. This guide is what stops that harvest turning into compost in September. Saving Your Own Seeds means next year's crop does not start with a purchase. Together they are a full year of food that runs on your labor and your ground rather than on anyone's permission, which is the entire point of the exercise. ## Sources The National Center for Home Food Preservation (which publishes the USDA's tested home canning procedures) and university extension services (Colorado State, Penn State, Iowa State): - https://nchfp.uga.edu/how/can/general-canning-information/ensuring-safe-canned-foods/ - https://nchfp.uga.edu/how/can/general-information/for-safetys-sake/ - https://nchfp.uga.edu/how/can/general-canning-information/using-boiling-water-canners/ - https://nchfp.uga.edu/how/can/how-do-i-can-tomatoes/tomato-acidification-directions/ - https://nchfp.uga.edu/how/can/how-do-i-can-tomatoes/crushed-tomatoes-with-no-added-liquid/ - https://nchfp.uga.edu/how/can/general-information/identifying-and-handling-spoiled-canned-food/ - https://nchfp.uga.edu/newsflash/canning-in-electric-multi-cookers - https://nchfp.uga.edu/resources/category/usda-guide (USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning, 2015 revision, free to download) - https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/freezing-vegetables/ - https://extension.psu.edu/lets-preserve-drying-fruits-and-vegetables-dehydration - https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/how-to/storing-winter-storage-vegetables - https://blogs.extension.iastate.edu/answerline/2021/08/03/the-case-for-bottled-lemon-juice-in-canning/ - https://blogs.extension.iastate.edu/answerline/2021/10/05/preserve-pumpkin-and-squash-safely/

docs.title: Your First Compost
headings: How you know it is done
docs.text: # Your First Compost Composting is letting food scraps and yard waste rot on purpose, in a controlled spot, until they turn back into dark, crumbly soil. You are not really doing the work; billions of bacteria and fungi are. Your whole job is to keep them fed, damp, and supplied with air. Do that even roughly right and you get free fertilizer while keeping waste out of the trash. Your first pile may go wrong. It may smell one week, sit cold the next, or take twice as long as you hoped. That is normal and useful: every problem has a smell or a look that tells you exactly what to fix, and this guide covers them all.
