Nobody composts perfectly the first time. ## What you need Cheap or free options first: - A spot of bare ground about 3 feet by 3 feet (roughly one big stride each way), or a container. Options, simplest first: - An open pile. Free. Works fine. Looks messy, and animals can reach it. - A homemade bin: a circle of wire fencing, a ring of pallets, or a plastic storage bin with air holes drilled in the sides. Nearly free. - A bought compost bin or a tumbler (a barrel on a stand that you spin to mix the contents). Costs money, but keeps animals out and mixing easy. Good for small yards. - No yard at all? A worm bin works indoors: red wiggler worms in a plastic tub about 21 by 15 inches, kept at 55 to 75 degrees F, eat your scraps and leave behind rich compost. It deserves its own guide; search "vermicomposting" plus your state university extension. - A garden fork, shovel, or sturdy stick for mixing. - A steady supply of two kinds of material, described next. ## Greens and browns Everything you compost is one of two kinds: - Greens are fresh and moist, and rich in nitrogen (the nutrient that feeds fast bacteria). Everyday examples: fruit and vegetable scraps, coffee grounds, tea bags (paper ones), crushed eggshells, fresh grass clippings. - Browns are dry and dead, and rich in carbon (the energy source). Everyday examples: dry autumn leaves, straw, shredded cardboard, shredded newspaper, small twigs, untreated wood chips or sawdust. The practical ratio: about 2 to 3 parts browns for every 1 part greens, measured by volume, not weight. A bucket of scraps means two to three buckets of leaves. You do not need to be exact; when in doubt, add more browns. Almost every compost problem is too many greens, not too few. ## What never goes in - Meat, fish, and bones: they attract rats and raccoons, and a home pile rarely gets hot enough to break them down safely. - Cheese, dairy, fats, oils, and grease: same reasons. - Dog or cat waste, and cat litter: pets can carry disease organisms that home compost does not reliably kill. - Diseased plants and weeds that have gone to seed (flowered and formed seed heads): a cool pile will not kill the disease or the seeds, and you will spread them later. - Treated or painted wood, and coal or barbecue ash: chemicals you do not want in your soil. ## Building and running the pile 1. Pick a spot with decent drainage, ideally on bare soil, out of any spot that floods. Shade or sun both work. 2. Start with a layer of bulky browns about 4 to 6 inches deep. Twiggy stuff at the very bottom helps air get in. 3. Add your greens. Chopping scraps into 1 to 2 inch pieces speeds everything up, because the bacteria work on surfaces. 4. Cover every addition of food scraps with 4 to 8 inches of browns. Buried food does not smell and does not attract animals. This one habit prevents most beginner problems. 5. Check moisture. Squeeze a handful of the mixed material from inside the pile (not the dry cover layer): it should feel like a wrung-out sponge, clearly damp but yielding at most a drop or two of water. Too dry, sprinkle water as you mix. Too wet, mix in dry browns. Gloves are a good habit, and always wash your hands after working the pile. 6. Turn the pile (mix it with a fork, bottom to top) every week or two if you want speed, or once or twice a month if you are patient. Turning feeds air to the bacteria. Skipping it does not ruin anything; it just slows things down. 7. Keep adding as scraps appear. When the pile reaches about 3 by 3 by 3 feet, it can hold enough heat inside to really cook. Smaller piles still compost, just slowly and coolly. A well-fed pile of that size warms up inside within days. The middle of a working pile feels distinctly hot to a quick touch; a compost thermometer will read about 130 to 160 degrees F (do not hold a bare hand in material that hot). Heat is a bonus, not a requirement: it speeds things up and helps kill weed seeds, but a cool pile still turns into compost eventually. ## The honest timeline Months, not weeks. Anyone promising two-week compost is selling something. - A tended pile (good ratio, kept damp, turned regularly): roughly 2 to 5 months. University sources vary in this range because climate, materials, and effort vary; warm weather is faster. - A well-managed tumbler: as little as a couple of months. The sealed container holds heat despite its small size, and spinning it makes the frequent mixing easy, which is why it can beat an open pile. - An ignored pile you just keep adding to: about a year, sometimes two. This is a legitimate method. Lazy composting works; it is only slow. After the pile stops heating, let it sit and finish for at least 4 more weeks (called curing). Half-finished compost can rob nitrogen from your plants instead of feeding them. ## How you know it is done Finished compost is dark brown, loose, and crumbly, smells like fresh earth after rain, and no longer looks like what you put in. The pile will have shrunk to about half its original height. A few stubborn bits (eggshells, avocado pits, corncobs) may remain; sift them out and toss them back into the next batch. ## Using it Spread a layer about 1/2 to 1 inch deep over garden beds and work it gently into the top of the soil, or ring it around existing plants, keeping it a few inches away from stems. Mix some into the soil when planting. Compost is far more forgiving than fertilizer, but more is not better: stick to the 1/2 to 1 inch a year. Years of heavy applications can build up excess nutrients in the soil. ## Troubleshooting - Smells like rotten eggs, rancid butter, or vinegar: not enough air, usually because the pile is too wet or packed down. Fluff and turn the whole pile and mix in dry browns. - Smells like ammonia (sharp, like window cleaner): too many greens. Mix in more browns. - Rats, raccoons, or other animals: something meaty, oily, or dairy got in, or food is sitting exposed. Remove it, always bury new scraps under browns, and if it continues, switch to a closed bin; cover any vent holes with fine metal mesh (hardware cloth). - Clouds of fruit flies: annoying, harmless. Bury scraps deeper under browns. Freezing scraps before adding them kills fruit fly eggs that ride in on fruit skins. - Pile will not heat up: it is too small (under about 3 by 3 by 3 feet), too dry, or too brown-heavy. Grow it, water it while turning, or mix in fresh greens like grass clippings. Or it may simply be finished; done compost runs cool. - Soggy mess: too much rain or too many wet greens. Turn it, add plenty of dry browns, and cover the top during long wet spells. - Bone dry and nothing happening: sprinkle water as you turn until it passes the wrung-out-sponge test. - Bugs, worms, and slugs everywhere inside the pile: good news, not a problem. They are decomposers doing the work. ## The loop this closes The scraps from your kitchen become the dark, living soil that a tomato seedling wants to grow in. Compost feeds the garden, the garden feeds you, and the trimmings go back into the pile. Waste stops being waste. Start the pile now and it will be ready for planting season. ## Sources - https://www.epa.gov/recycle/composting-home - https://extension.umn.edu/managing-soil-and-nutrients/composting-home-gardens - https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/extension-gardener-handbook/2-composting - https://extension.unh.edu/resource/composting-home-gardener-fact-sheet - https://ccetompkins.org/resources/compost-troubleshooting-your-compost - https://extension.umd.edu/resource/indoor-worm-composting-or-vermicomposting

docs.title: Collecting Rainwater
headings: Second: this water is not for drinking
How much water a roof really makes
Check your roof before you start
Build the base like it matters, because it does
First flush: the first water off the roof is the dirtiest
Plan the overflow before the first storm
docs.text: # Collecting Rainwater Rain that lands on your roof runs into the gutters, down a pipe called a downspout, and away into the ground. A rain barrel is simply a container parked under that downspout to catch some of the water before it leaves. The reward is free water for your garden, less mud around your house in storms, and a small buffer of non-drinking water for emergencies. This is one of the easiest projects in this series. The hard parts are not the plumbing; they are the safety details around weight, mosquitoes, and where the extra water goes. This guide covers all of them. ## First: check your local rules Rainwater law is not the same everywhere. In most of the United States you may collect freely, but a few states regulate or limit it because of how water rights work there. Colorado, for example, allows single-family homes (and multifamily buildings of four or fewer units) only two barrels holding 110 gallons combined, with sealable lids, used outdoors on the same property (see the Colorado State University Extension page in Sources). Other countries have their own rules. Before you buy anything, search your state or local government website for "rain barrel" or "rainwater harvesting," or ask your local university extension office. This takes ten minutes and can save you a fine. ## Second: this water is not for drinking Roof water picks up bird droppings, dust, insect remains, and traces of the roof itself. University extension guidance is consistent: water from a rain barrel is non-potable, which means not safe to drink, and should not be used for drinking, cooking, or brushing teeth. This guide is for watering ornamental plants, washing tools and muddy boots, and other non-drinking uses. For actual drinking water storage, use the Storing Water Safely guide in this series; do not try to make roof water drinkable. One honest disagreement to know about: extension services differ on using rain barrel water on food gardens. Nebraska Extension recommends keeping it off fruits and vegetables entirely. The cautious path, and the one this guide takes: use rain barrel water on flowers, shrubs, trees, and lawn, and keep tap water for anything you will eat. ## How much water a roof really makes The math is simple and the answer surprises everyone. One inch of rain falling on one square foot of roof yields about 0.6 gallons of water (0.623 to be exact). Worked example: a modest 1,200 square foot roof in a one inch rainstorm sheds about 750 gallons (1,200 x 1 x 0.623). If one downspout drains a quarter of that roof, about 300 square feet, it delivers nearly 190 gallons per inch of rain, which means about a third of an inch of rain fills a standard 55 gallon barrel. A barrel fills much faster than intuition says, which is why the overflow section below matters. ## What you need Cheapest options first. - A barrel, 50 to 55 gallons is the standard size. A recycled food-grade barrel (one that held food or drink ingredients, sold cheaply by feed stores, soda bottlers, and farmers, or found on local marketplaces; avoid barrels that held meat products) works as well as a bought rain barrel. Never use a barrel that held chemicals, soaps, or anything unknown; residue can poison your soil and you cannot rinse away what you cannot identify. Dark, opaque barrels are best because sunlight through light-colored plastic grows algae; a light barrel can be painted a dark color. - A spigot (faucet) kit for the bottom of the barrel, or a purpose-made rain barrel that already has one, plus an overflow fitting near the top. Hardware stores sell simple kits. - Fiberglass window screen, enough to cover every opening. - Concrete blocks or a purpose-built stand for a raised, level base. - A hacksaw for shortening the downspout, and a drill if your barrel needs holes cut. Safety glasses and gloves for the cutting. - Optional but worthwhile: a first flush diverter (explained below) and a flexible downspout elbow to aim water into the barrel. ## Check your roof before you start Nebraska Extension's list of roof materials that can shed chemicals into runoff includes asphalt roofing, redwood or cedar shakes, treated wood shingles, roofing containing asbestos, lead solder or lead-based paint, zinc from galvanized flashing, and moss-killer treatments. That list includes the most common roof in America, so here is the honest practical reading: extension rain-barrel programs across the country assume ordinary asphalt-shingle roofs, because for the ornamental-and-garden watering this guide allows, shingle runoff is broadly treated as acceptable. The list is why the no-drinking rule exists, and why the riskier materials below deserve real caution. If your roof is old enough that asbestos is possible, or it has been treated with moss killer, or you simply do not know what it is made of, do not collect from it until you find out. Zinc anti-moss strips near the ridge are a common quiet offender; look for thin metal strips running along the roof peak. ## Build the base like it matters, because it does Water weighs almost 8.5 pounds per gallon. A full 55 gallon barrel weighs about 460 pounds. That is not a thing you can catch if it tips, and a falling barrel can seriously injure a child or pet standing next to it. So: 1. Choose ground that is firm and can be made level. Soft soil under 460 pounds will settle unevenly and lean. 2. Build a platform from solid concrete blocks (not stacked bricks that can shift) one or two courses high. Raising the barrel makes room for a watering can under the spigot and improves the gravity flow. 3. Check the platform with a level side to side and front to back before the barrel goes on. Fix it now; you cannot fix it full. 4. Never let children climb on or hang from the barrel, and do not stack anything on top. 5. **Treat it as open water.** Fifty gallons standing at toddler height is a drowning hazard to a small child or a pet, independent of every other risk on this page. The lid and the screens stay secured at all times, not just in mosquito season. Draw water from the spigot; never open the barrel to dip a can into it. ## Setting it up 1. Set the empty barrel on its finished base, directly under or beside the downspout. 2. With the barrel in place, hold the downspout elbow where it will sit, aimed at the barrel inlet, and mark the downspout about two inches below the top of the elbow (the Rutgers Extension method: measure with the elbow held in position, never against the bare inlet, because the elbow itself adds several inches of drop). Take the barrel away and cut the downspout at the mark with the hacksaw. Wear safety glasses; cut metal edges are sharp, so file or tape them. If the cut requires a ladder or the gutters need repair, hire a gutter company rather than balance a saw overhead. Ladder falls are the serious injury in this project. 3. Squeeze the freshly cut end slightly with pliers if needed and push the elbow onto it, secured with short downspout screws, so water aims into the barrel inlet. Keep the removed section; you will want it back in winter. 4. Fit the spigot near the bottom and the overflow fitting near the top, following the kit instructions. 5. Cover the inlet and every other opening with window screen pulled tight and secured. No gaps, ever. This is doing two jobs: it is your mosquito defense, and it is the barrier that keeps a child or an animal out of the water. Extension guidance gives the second reason first. Some jurisdictions add their own container rules on top (Colorado, for example, requires barrels to have a sealable lid). 6. Attach a hose to the overflow fitting, at least 8 to 10 feet long, and run it where you want storm water to go (next section). ## First flush: the first water off the roof is the dirtiest Between rains, droppings and dust build up on the roof, and the first minutes of a storm rinse almost all of it off. A first flush diverter is a simple standpipe on the downspout that fills with that first dirty water and then routes the rest, cleaner, to your barrel. Texas A&M recommends diverting about 1 to 2 gallons for every 100 square feet of roof feeding your barrel, and emptying the diverter chamber after each rain so it is ready for the next one. A diverter is optional for a garden barrel, but it noticeably improves water clarity and smell for a few dollars of PVC pipe. ## Plan the overflow before the first storm Remember the arithmetic: a third of an inch of rain fills the barrel, and a real storm keeps going. Hundreds of gallons will pass through the overflow, and water dumped beside your house finds its way into basements and crawl spaces. Rutgers Extension says to direct overflow at least 6 feet from the foundation if you have a basement, at least 2 feet if you have a crawl space; farther is better, and it should flow downhill away from the house, into a garden bed, a lawn, or the base of a tree. Watch it work during the first heavy rain and adjust. ## Using the water Honesty about pressure: a rain barrel is gravity-fed, and gravity a few feet up delivers far less pressure than a house spigot. Sprinklers will not run from a barrel. What works: filling watering cans (the simplest and best method, per Nebraska Extension), drip or soaker hoses designed for rain barrels, and letting a hose trickle at the base of a plant. Raising the barrel on its base helps. Use the water within a few days after rain; that empties the barrel for the next storm and denies mosquitoes a nursery. ## Winter care Where it freezes, water left in the barrel will expand and crack it. Before hard freezes: drain the barrel completely, disconnect it, reattach the downspout piece you saved (or add an extension) so winter melt still drains away from the foundation, and store the barrel upside down, covered, or in a shed with the spigot open. ## Cleaning Once a year, usually when you shut down for winter, scrub the inside with a long-handled brush and rinse. For lingering smells, Alabama Extension suggests 2 teaspoons of castile soap plus 2 teaspoons of lemon juice or vinegar per gallon of wash water, and advises against bleach or harsh commercial cleaners because the residue ends up in your soil. Rinse until the water runs clear. ## What can go wrong - Wiggling little larvae in the water: mosquitoes got past a gap. In warm weather they can go from egg to adult in as little as 5 to 7 days, so act the day you see them. Find and fix the screen gap, and use or dump the water. If water routinely sits more than about 72 hours, check for larvae; a Bti mosquito dunk (a bacterial larva killer sold at garden stores, labeled for rain barrels) is a safe backstop, but tight screens are the real fix. - Green water or green film: algae, fed by sunlight through the barrel wall. Move the barrel to shade or paint it a dark color, and scrub it out at the next cleaning. - Rotten-egg or swampy smell: water sat too long with debris in it, often leaves that got past the inlet screen. Drain it onto the lawn, clean the barrel, add or repair the inlet screen, and consider a first flush diverter. - Barrel always empty: your downspout may drain a smaller roof section than you thought, or the elbow is missing the inlet in wind-blown rain. Watch it during a storm. If it truly fills and empties fast, that is success; add a second barrel in series (its inlet fed by the first barrel's overflow hose) if your rules allow. - Barrel leaning: drain it immediately and fix the base. Never try to shim a full barrel. ## How you know it worked After a storm, the barrel is full, the overflow ran away from the house, and nothing leans. A week later the water is clear-ish, smells like nothing much, and has no wigglers in it. Your watering cans fill themselves for free all summer, and when you tip the barrel over in late fall, cleaning it takes ten minutes. That is the whole win: a quiet system that mostly tends itself. ## Sources University extension services and a state extension legal summary: - https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g2220/na/html/view - https://njaes.rutgers.edu/fs1118/ - https://njaes.rutgers.edu/fs1240/ - https://rainwaterharvesting.tamu.edu/pre-storage-treatment/ - https://www.aces.edu/blog/topics/fish-water/chapter-4-diy-rain-barrel-construction/ - https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/rainwater-collection-in-colorado

docs.title: Storing Water Safely
headings: What you need (cheap or free options first)
Step 1: Clean and sanitize the container
How to tell stored water has gone bad
docs.text: # Storing Water Safely If the tap stopped working tonight, how long could your household drink, cook, and wash? Storing water is one of the cheapest, simplest preparedness skills there is, and it is very hard to get wrong if you follow a few exact rules from public health agencies. This guide uses the numbers published by the CDC (the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) and the EPA (the US Environmental Protection Agency), plus university extension services. Where a number matters, it is theirs, not ours. This guide is for emergency preparedness. It is not a substitute for guidance from your local health department or water utility. If they issue instructions during a real emergency (a boil-water advisory, for example), follow their instructions first. ## How much water to store The CDC's rule: store at least 1 gallon (about 4 liters) of water per person per day, for at least 3 days. That gallon covers drinking, cooking, and basic washing. If you can, aim for a 2-week supply. Store more than that if anyone in the household is pregnant or sick, or if you live in a hot climate. Ohio State University Extension suggests about 1 quart (roughly a liter) a day for a small pet. Quick math for a family of four: 4 people x 1 gallon x 14 days = 56 gallons for the full 2-week goal. That sounds like a lot, but it is fourteen 4-gallon stackable containers, or a mix of jugs and bottled water built up a little at a time. Start with 3 days (12 gallons) and grow from there. ## What you need (cheap or free options first) - Unopened store-bought bottled water. The CDC calls this the safest and most reliable emergency water. Watch the expiration date on the label. - Empty 2-liter soda bottles, washed well. Utah State University Extension says these are acceptable because they are less likely to leak or hold food residues. - Food-grade water containers (the blue 5 to 7 gallon jugs from camping or surplus stores). "Food grade" means the plastic is made to hold food or water without transferring harmful substances into it. - One bottle of plain unscented liquid household chlorine bleach. The label should say it contains between 5% and 9% sodium hypochlorite (the active chlorine chemical). No scents, no "splashless," no added cleaners. - A medicine dropper (for measuring bleach by the drop), a permanent marker, and some masking tape for labels. ### Containers to never use - Milk jugs and juice bottles. Milk proteins and fruit sugars soak into the plastic and cannot be fully washed out; they feed bacteria in your stored water. The thin plastic also cracks and leaks over time. - Anything that ever held a toxic chemical: bleach bottles, pesticide jugs, fuel cans, cleaning product containers. The CDC says do not use these, period. No amount of rinsing makes them safe. - Glass works but breaks; the CDC recommends durable, unbreakable containers with a tight-closing lid, ideally with a narrow neck so you pour instead of dipping. ## Step 1: Clean and sanitize the container This is the CDC's exact procedure. "Sanitize" means killing the germs that washing alone leaves behind. 1. Wash the container with soap and water, then rinse completely. 2. Mix a sanitizing solution: 1 teaspoon of unscented 5% to 9% household bleach in 1 quart (about 1 liter) of water. This mix is for rinsing the container only; it is far too strong to drink. Disinfecting drinking water uses only DROPS of bleach (see the disinfection section further down). 3. Pour the solution into the container, close the lid tightly, and shake well so the solution touches every inside surface. 4. Wait at least 30 seconds, then pour the solution out. 5. Let the container air-dry, or rinse it with water that is already safe (treated tap water or bottled water). Do not rinse with untreated water, which would re-contaminate it. ## Step 2: Fill it - From a treated municipal supply (city tap water): fill the sanitized container straight from the tap and cap it tightly. City water is already disinfected, so nothing more is needed. - From any other source (well, spring, rain barrel, or a tap under a boil-water advisory): treat the water FIRST using the disinfection section below, then fill. ## Step 3: Store it right - Label every container "drinking water" with the date you filled it. - Keep it cool: the CDC recommends 50 to 70 degrees Fahrenheit (10 to 21 degrees Celsius). A closet, basement, or under-bed space works. - Keep it dark. Never store water in direct sunlight; light feeds algae growth and ages plastic. - Keep it away from gasoline, pesticides, and other chemicals. Vapors can pass slowly through plastic. - Keep it off bare concrete. Utah State University Extension recommends storing containers off the ground and off cement; a scrap board or wooden pallet costs nothing and also protects against temperature swings from the slab. - Freezer bonus: a few bottles in the freezer (leave 2 to 3 inches of air space so they do not burst) give you ice during a power outage and become drinking water as they melt. ## Rotation: the 6-month rule Replace water you filled yourself every 6 months. This is the CDC's number, and Utah State and Ohio State extensions give the same figure. Rotation day is a good time to re-sanitize containers and to replace your stored bleach bottle too, since bleach quietly loses strength as it ages. Store-bought bottled water just follows its printed expiration date. An easy habit: rotate when the clocks change, or on New Year's Day and the Fourth of July. Old stored water is not wasted; use it on plants or for cleaning. ## How to tell stored water has gone bad Look and smell before you drink: - Cloudiness or floating particles that were not there when you filled it - Green tinge or slime (algae) on the water or container walls - A rotten or sour smell - A bulging or leaking container If you see any of these, do not drink it. Dump it, re-sanitize the container (Step 1), and refill. Perfectly stored water can still taste flat or faintly of plastic; that alone does not mean it is unsafe (see troubleshooting below). ## Disinfecting questionable water Use this when you must drink water you are not sure about: an untreated source, or stored water during an emergency when you cannot simply dump and refill. If the water is cloudy, first let it settle and pour the clear part through a clean cloth, paper towel, or coffee filter. Boiling (the most reliable method): - Bring water to a rolling boil for at least 1 minute. - At high altitude, boil for 3 minutes. The EPA sets this cutoff at altitudes above 5,000 feet; the CDC uses 6,500 feet. The agencies differ, so if you live above 5,000 feet the safe choice is the full 3 minutes. - Let it cool before drinking. Bleach (when you cannot boil), the EPA's exact table, using plain unscented household bleach: - If the label says 6% sodium hypochlorite: 2 drops per quart or liter, 8 drops per gallon. - If the label says 8.25% sodium hypochlorite: 2 drops per quart or liter, 6 drops per gallon. - Double the amount if the water is still cloudy or colored after settling and filtering, or if it is very cold. - Stir, cover, and let it stand for 30 minutes. The water should have a slight chlorine smell. If it does not, repeat the dose and let it stand another 15 minutes before use. The CDC's simplified version is consistent: 8 drops (a little less than 1/8 teaspoon) of 5% to 9% bleach per gallon of clear water, 16 drops (1/4 teaspoon) if cloudy, stand at least 30 minutes. (For 8.25% bleach the CDC rounds slightly higher than the EPA table; either dose is safe.) Note what bleach and boiling do NOT fix: chemical contamination (fuel, pesticides, industrial spills). If water smells of chemicals, no home treatment makes it drinkable; find another source. One more gap worth knowing, because bleach is not the universal answer it looks like: chlorine and iodine do not reliably kill the parasite *Cryptosporidium*. The CDC states that iodine or chlorine tablets "kill most germs, but will not kill Cryptosporidium germs." Boiling does kill it, and so do chlorine dioxide tablets and a filter with an absolute pore size of 1 micron or smaller. If you are treating water from an unknown source rather than refreshing your own stored supply, read the companion guide, Making Water Safe to Drink, which covers the pathogen classes, what filters do and do not remove, and how to combine methods. ## What can go wrong (honest troubleshooting) - Plastic or flat taste. Common and usually harmless; water stored without air goes flat. Pour it back and forth between two clean containers to put air back in (a standard extension-service tip for boiled or stored water). If a strong chemical taste persists, the container may not be food grade; discard the water and retire that container from water duty. - Green growth. Algae got light. Dump the water, re-sanitize the container, refill, and move it somewhere truly dark. Do not just top it off; the growth clings to the walls. - Cloudy stored water. Something got in, often from dipping hands or a dirty scoop. Dump, re-sanitize, refill. In future, pour instead of dipping, and never touch the inside of the container or lid. - You forgot to rotate and it is 14 months old. Do not panic and do not drink it untreated. If it looks and smells fine it is probably safe, but the cautious move outside an emergency is to rotate it now. In an actual emergency, disinfect it (previous section) before drinking. Your first attempt may go sideways: a leaky jug, a forgotten label, a bottle that tastes like a pool toy. That is normal and useful. Every failure teaches you before the day it matters. ## How you know it worked - You can point to at least 1 gallon per person per day for 3 or more days, in labeled, dated, tightly capped containers. - The water is clear, smells like nothing (or very faintly of chlorine), and the containers show no growth or leaks. - Every label is less than 6 months old. - A bottle of unscented 5% to 9% bleach and a dropper sit next to the water, ready for disinfection if you ever need it. When all four are true, your household has real water security for the most common emergencies. Quiet peace of mind, earned in an afternoon. ## Sources - https://www.cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/how-to-create-and-store-an-emergency-water-supply.html - https://www.cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/index.html - https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/emergency-disinfection-drinking-water - https://extension.usu.edu/preparedness/articles-and-research/storing-water-for-an-emergency - https://ohioline.osu.edu/factsheet/hyg-5354 - https://www.ready.gov/water

docs.title: Making Water Safe to Drink
headings: Start by choosing the best source you can
Step 1: clear it first (this is not treatment)
Step 2: boiling, the one that always works
Step 3: filters, and the pore size that decides everything
The combination that covers the most ground
After treatment: do not put it back where it came from
docs.text: # Making Water Safe to Drink There is water in front of you and you do not know whether it is safe. It might be a stream, a well after a flood, a rain barrel, a tap under a boil-water advisory, or a jug that has been in the garage since you cannot remember when. This guide is about that moment: how to decide what is wrong with the water, which treatment fixes that particular thing, and which problems no home treatment fixes at all. Its companion, Storing Water Safely, covers the calmer half of the subject: how much to store, what containers to use, how to sanitize and label them, and how to rotate the supply. If you are filling containers from a working, treated tap, that guide is the one you want and this one is not needed. Come here when the source is questionable. The two guides overlap deliberately on boiling and bleach, because those two facts are worth knowing twice. One honest thing first. "Purifying water" is not one job, it is three separate jobs, and no single method does all three: 1. **Germs** (bacteria, viruses, parasites). These are what make people acutely ill within days, and they are what most treatment addresses. 2. **Dirt** (silt, leaves, cloudiness). Mostly a nuisance, but it interferes with the methods that handle germs. 3. **Chemicals** (fuel, pesticides, industrial spills, lead, nitrate, arsenic). These are the ones home treatment largely cannot touch, and the ones people most often assume boiling handles. Sort out which one you actually have before you do anything. ## Start by choosing the best source you can Treatment is a last resort, not a first move. Before treating, look for better water. A covered well is better than an open pond. Water upstream of a settlement is better than water downstream of it. Rain caught in a clean container is better than runoff. Clear is better than cloudy. Flowing is better than standing. And the one absolute rule, in CDC's words: "You cannot make water containing fuel, toxic chemicals, or radioactive materials safe by boiling or disinfecting it." If the water smells of fuel or solvent, or if you know an industrial or agricultural spill has reached it, no technique in this guide applies. Find another source. ## Step 1: clear it first (this is not treatment) Cloudy water defeats chemical disinfection, because the disinfectant is used up on the particles, and germs shelter inside clumps of sediment. CDC's method: let the water settle, then filter it through a clean cloth, paper towel, or coffee filter, and draw off the clear part. That does not make it safe. Nothing that removes visible dirt makes water safe. It makes the actual treatment work. ## Step 2: boiling, the one that always works If you can boil, boil. It handles all three classes of germ, it needs no special equipment, and it cannot be done wrong except by not doing it long enough. - CDC: "Bring clear water to a rolling boil for 1 minute (at elevations above 6,500 feet, boil for 3 minutes)." - EPA puts the altitude cutoff lower, above 5,000 feet. The agencies differ, so above 5,000 feet the safe choice is the full 3 minutes. - WHO, whose guidance covers the whole world rather than one country, states that "heating water to a rolling boil, as recommended in the WHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality, is sufficient to inactivate pathogenic bacteria, viruses and protozoa." Note the WHO wording carefully. It is the *rolling boil* that is the signal, not the number of minutes. The visible rolling boil tells you the water reached a disinfecting temperature; you do not need a thermometer, which is exactly why the method is so robust. CDC's travel guidance notes that lower temperatures also work with longer contact, with temperatures as low as 60 C (140 F) effective over 30 minutes, but at home you do not have a way to verify 60 C, and you can see a boil from across the room. Let it cool covered. Boiled water tastes flat because the dissolved air has been driven off; pouring it back and forth between two clean containers puts the air back. **What boiling does not do:** it does not remove chemicals. Worse, it concentrates them, because the water leaves as steam and the chemical stays behind. CDC states it plainly for lead: "Boiling this water will not reduce the amount of lead in your water." ## Step 3: filters, and the pore size that decides everything This is where most confusion lives. A filter is a sieve, so whether it works depends entirely on whether its holes are smaller than the thing you are trying to catch. Germs differ enormously in size, and no single number covers them. CDC's travel health guidance gives the sizes: - **Viruses** are about 0.03 micrometers across, and need a pore size of about 0.01 to catch them, which means an ultrafilter. - **Bacteria** such as E. coli are 0.5 by 2 to 8 micrometers, and need a pore size of 0.2 to 0.4 or smaller. - ***Cryptosporidium***, a parasite, is 4 to 6 micrometers, and needs a pore size of 1 or smaller. - ***Giardia***, a parasite, is 8 by 19 micrometers, and needs a pore size of 3 to 5 or smaller. A micrometer, also called a micron, is a thousandth of a millimeter. The practical consequence of those sizes is this ladder: - **Microfilters**, pores under 1 micron: the ordinary hiking and camping filter. Removes bacteria and parasites. CDC: microfilters "do not reliably remove enteric viruses." Good for a clean wilderness stream. Not good enough on its own where human sewage may have reached the water. - **Ultrafilters**, about 0.01 micron: CDC describes these as "effective for removing viruses, bacteria, and parasites." This is the level at which a filter alone handles all three classes of germ. - **Nanofilters and reverse osmosis:** remove viruses and, unlike everything above, also remove chemical contaminants. This is the only filtration class in ordinary reach that touches problem 3. - **Activated carbon** (the black granules in most household filter pitchers): CDC is precise here, carbon filters "trap, but do not kill, microorganisms." What they do well is remove chlorine, iodine, heavy metals, and bad taste. A carbon pitcher filter is not a treatment for unsafe water and was never sold as one. CDC's emergency guidance for choosing a portable filter: it needs "an absolute pore size of 1 micron or smaller to remove parasites (such as *Giardia* or *Cryptosporidium*)," and such a filter "will not remove viruses." **How to read a filter's label.** Two things matter. First, look for **absolute** pore size, not nominal; a nominal rating is an average, and an average pore size of 1 micron means some pores are larger. Second, look for what it is certified to remove. A product marketed in the United States as a water **purifier** has to demonstrate, under EPA's guidance, removal of "at least 99.9999% of bacteria, 99.99% of viruses, and 99.9% of *Cryptosporidium* oocysts or *Giardia* cysts." A product marketed as a **filter** makes no such claim about viruses. If you buy one thing after reading this guide, buy the filter whose label says what it removes, and keep the label. ## Step 4: chemical disinfection Use this when you cannot boil: no fuel, no power, or you need to treat a large volume. **Household bleach.** Plain and unscented, labeled as sodium hypochlorite, with nothing else added. Not scented, not "splashless," not color-safe, not a bleach with detergent or cleaners mixed in, and not pool chlorine. If the label lists anything beyond sodium hypochlorite and water, do not put it in drinking water. CDC's amounts for 5 to 9 percent bleach: - **1 quart or 1 liter of water:** 2 drops of bleach. - **1 gallon:** 8 drops, a little less than 1/8 teaspoon. - **5 gallons:** 40 drops, about 2.5 mL. Double the amount if the water is cloudy, colored or very cold. Stir, cover, and let it stand at least 30 minutes before drinking. The water should have a slight chlorine smell afterward; if it does not, repeat the dose and wait another 15 minutes. EPA's table is equivalent, differing only in that it gives 6 drops per gallon for 8.25 percent bleach and 8 drops per gallon for 6 percent. Storing Water Safely has more on selecting and storing the bleach itself, including the fact that bleach loses strength as it ages and should be replaced along with your stored water. **Iodine.** EPA: add 5 drops of 2 percent tincture of iodine per quart or liter, or 10 drops if the water is cloudy or colored, then stir and let it stand at least 30 minutes. Iodine has medical limits that chlorine does not; read the product label, and if you are pregnant, have a thyroid condition, or have an iodine sensitivity, ask a clinician before using it. It is also not meant for continuous long-term use. **Chlorine dioxide tablets.** These matter for one specific reason, in the next section. Follow the product label exactly; strengths and contact times differ between products, and the contact time is often much longer than for bleach. **The gap you have to know about.** Chlorine and iodine do not reliably kill *Cryptosporidium*. CDC states it directly: "Iodine, tablets with iodine, or chlorine tablets kill most germs, but will not kill Cryptosporidium germs." CDC's travel guidance explains why: the parasite is "poorly inactivated by chlorine- or iodine-based disinfection at practical concentrations." So a jug treated with bleach is not automatically safe from everything. Two things do handle *Cryptosporidium*: boiling, and chlorine dioxide, which CDC says "kills waterborne pathogens, including *Cryptosporidium* oocysts, at practical doses and contact times." A filter of 1 micron absolute or smaller catches it physically. ## The combination that covers the most ground Match the method to what you are worried about: - **Bacteria:** boiling yes, microfilter yes, bleach or iodine yes, chlorine dioxide yes. - **Viruses:** boiling yes, microfilter **no**, bleach or iodine yes, chlorine dioxide yes. - **Giardia:** boiling yes, microfilter yes, chlorine dioxide yes, bleach or iodine **less reliable**. - **Cryptosporidium:** boiling yes, microfilter yes, chlorine dioxide yes, bleach or iodine **no**. - **Chemicals:** boiling **no**, microfilter **no**, bleach or iodine **no**, chlorine dioxide **no**. ("Microfilter" here means a filter with an absolute pore size under 1 micron, the ordinary camping kind.) On the *Giardia* line, the two CDC sources differ in emphasis and the cautious reading is the one above. CDC's travel guidance treats chlorine and iodine as effective against *Giardia* given adequate contact time; CDC's emergency guidance says more plainly that disinfectants "do not work as well as boiling for killing some germs, including the parasites *Cryptosporidium* and *Giardia*." Treat bleach as an imperfect answer for both parasites and use boiling, a filter, or chlorine dioxide where you can. Reading down that list, boiling is the only single method that covers every germ line, which is why it stays the first recommendation whenever fuel exists. When it does not, the strong pairing is **filter, then disinfect**: a microfilter takes out the parasites and the cloudiness that would otherwise consume the chemical, and the chemical then handles the viruses the filter let through. CDC's own phrasing on filters is the warning label for doing only half of this: "Filtered water might need additional treatment to be safe." Note the entirely empty bottom line. That is the point of the next section. ## What nothing here fixes No method in this guide removes chemical contamination. Not boiling, not a camping filter, not bleach, not a carbon pitcher. That covers fuel and solvent spills, pesticides, industrial discharge, and also the quieter ones that have no smell at all: lead from old plumbing, nitrate from fertilizer runoff, arsenic in some groundwater. For lead specifically, CDC recommends a point-of-use filter certified by an independent testing organization, one whose label shows "NSF/ANSI standard 53 for lead removal and NSF/ANSI standard 42 for particulate removal," and notes that you should draw water for drinking and cooking only from the cold tap, because warm or hot tap water "can have higher levels of lead." The general answers to chemical contamination are reverse osmosis, certain certified filters, or a different source. The general answer to "is there a chemical problem in my water" is a laboratory test, not a taste or a smell. If you are on a private well, your local health department or extension office can tell you what to test for and where. Two methods that are worth knowing exist but that this guide deliberately does not teach, because doing them properly requires more than a paragraph: - **Solar disinfection (SODIS)**, which uses sunlight in clear plastic bottles and matters greatly where fuel is scarce or expensive. WHO evaluates household water treatment technologies including this one; start from their drinking-water quality guidance rather than from a summary. - **Distillation**, which is the one home method that separates water from dissolved chemicals and salts. It is slow, fuel-hungry, and has its own procedure. ## After treatment: do not put it back where it came from Treated water in a dirty container is untreated water again. Pour it into a container that has been washed and sanitized, cap it tightly, label it with the date, and keep it cool and dark. Storing Water Safely covers sanitizing containers step by step, which containers never to use (milk jugs, and anything that held a chemical), and the six-month rotation rule. If you treated the water because of a boil-water advisory, keep treating until your water utility says the advisory is lifted, and follow their instructions over anything written here. They know what happened to the system; a general guide does not. ## What can go wrong - **The water still tastes and smells of chlorine.** Normal after disinfection, and a slight chlorine smell is the confirmation that the dose was enough. Let it stand uncovered for a while, or pour it between clean containers, or run it through a carbon filter, which is the one job a carbon pitcher does very well. - **You treated cloudy water and someone got sick anyway.** The classic chemical-disinfection failure. The particles consumed the chlorine and sheltered the germs. Always settle and pre-filter first, and double the dose for cloudy water. - **You used a hiking filter on water downstream of a town.** A microfilter does not remove viruses. Boil it, or add a chemical step, or use a filter rated as a purifier. - **The filter clogged or slowed to a trickle.** That is what a working filter does as it fills up. Backflush or replace the element per the instructions, and pre-filter cloudy water to make the element last. Never scrape or "clean" a filter element in a way the maker does not describe; you can open channels straight through it. - **You boiled water that had a chemical smell.** Do not drink it. You concentrated the problem. Discard it and find another source. - **A jug tastes like the container.** It may not be food grade. Retire it from water duty. Storing Water Safely lists containers to never use. - **You cannot remember whether that jug was treated.** Then it was not. Label everything, always, at the moment you fill it. ## How you know it worked - You can name which of the three problems you were solving, and the method you used is one that actually addresses it. - Water that started cloudy was settled and pre-filtered before any chemical went in. - If you used a filter, you know its absolute pore size and what its label says it removes. - If you used bleach, the water had a faint chlorine smell after 30 minutes. - The treated water is now in a clean, sanitized, labeled, dated, tightly capped container, stored cool and dark. - If there is any chance of chemical contamination, you did not treat it at all. You went and found different water. That last one is the most important line in this guide. Almost everything about drinking water is a solvable problem with a known procedure. The one that is not solvable at home is the one worth recognizing, and recognizing it is a skill in itself. ## Sources US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, US Environmental Protection Agency, and the World Health Organization: - https://www.cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/index.html - https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/preparing-international-travelers/water-disinfection-for-travelers.html - https://www.cdc.gov/lead-prevention/prevention/drinking-water.html - https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/emergency-disinfection-drinking-water - https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-FWC-WSH-15.02 (WHO technical brief, "Boil water") - https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549950 (WHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality)
